Watergate, A Hoax?
desc:
Watergate, A Hoax?

Authored by Silvio Canto, Jr. via American Thinker,

If you are a baby boomer, you remember The Beatles, Henry Aaron hitting #715, and President Nixon resigning over Watergate. It was our soundtrack, as they like to say. It gave us words like "Nixonian" and "The Saturday Night Massacre" and Oval Office tapes. It turned the 37th president into an evil man, and everyone took a shot at him. Even the GOP took down his pictures at the party's convention.

As someone who admired President Nixon, bought and read all of his post presidency books, and volunteered as a student for his 1972 reelection campaign, I do believe that revisiting Watergate is a good idea. Maybe The Washington Post will end up returning that Pulitzer? Don't bet on that, but who knows?

What if Watergate was a hoax, as we say these days? Honestly, after watching Russiagate, the New York trials, and everything else, the idea is not so crazy. I'm not ready to call it a hoax yet, but I'm open to a conversation, as they say these days.

Well, some people think so, such as John D. O'Connor:

Many citizens today, with varied sources of information, understand the highly unethical lawfare waged against President Donald Trump, as exemplified by the Russiagate hoax. By contrast, the more restricted media environment of the early 1970s made prosecutorial misconduct during Watergate harder to scrutinize. With fresh eyes now taking a closer look at the reporting and prosecution of Watergate, it is becoming clear that DOJ investigators should sanction prosecutorial misconduct and set the historical record straight on Richard Nixon's innocence.

As a refresher, Watergate refers to a political scandal stemming from the June 17, 1972, burglary of the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate building by burglars with known CIA ties. After two years of investigations, committee inquiries, and trials, over 40 government officials were convicted or jailed, and President Richard Nixon was forced to resign from office.

Recently, former Nixon aide and historian Geoff Shepard presented his case to the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR), arguing that the proceedings against Richard Nixon amounted to dishonest, partisan "lawfare" enabled by prosecutorial and Congressional misconduct. Hopefully, the OPR will follow up with a vigorous investigation and clear the record of this unfairly maligned former president.

Clear the record of this unfairly maligned former president? Yes, it's time for a second look at that whole story.

As the article points out:

Why, fifty years later, should we investigate any flaws in Nixon's prosecution? Because key questions remain: 1) was the prosecution of Nixon and aides (with Nixon as an unindicted co-conspirator) so clearly unethical that the OPR should conclude formally that the prosecution was fatally and unethically flawed;

and 2) were the Senate investigation and Majority Watergate Report false in material particulars, constituting a willfully false official Report to the public? In light of the attempted replay of Watergate and the Russiagate hoax, these questions are existential.

Bring it on. Maybe it's time to revisit that whole episode that consumed the country for years. I do recall people back then, such as a neighbor historian, saying that there was a lot of hypocrisy in these attacks against President Nixon. I do believe that the collapse of Vietnam and the betrayal of the Shah of Iran would have turned out differently if President Nixon had been in the Oval Office.

So, let's open up the case and hear more about this.

title: US Firms Account For 75% Of Chips Powering Russia's New Jet Drone
desc:
US Firms Account For 75% Of Chips Powering Russia's New Jet Drone

Building on our earlier notes mapping out the supply chain behind the Russian one-way attack drone, a new report from a Ukrainian defense news outlet claims that a whopping "three-quarters of the Geran-4's onboard computer consists of electronic components manufactured by American companies."

Militarnyi's supply-chain intelligence investigation into Russian Geran-4 drones identified 80 components from US companies among 105 cataloged parts, suggesting how heavily Russia relies on foreign technology despite severe sanctions from Western governments.

An engineering unit with Ukraine's 1230th Athena Engineering and Technical Regiment examined the chips, recovered from recent Geran-4 drone wreckage with most internal components intact, allowing investigators to inspect markings and serial numbers to identify manufacturers.

Here's what they found:

After comparing board descriptions and manufacturer lists, the researcher was able to identify 105 electronic components. Of these, at least 80 are from American companies, accounting for 76.19% of the total.

Countries are determined based on the parent company's place of registration. Under this approach, Intersil components are classified as products of the Japanese company Renesas, while Zetex components are classified as products of the American company Diodes Incorporated.

Texas Instruments dominates the list of manufacturers by a wide margin. Together with National Semiconductor, which it acquired in 2011, the two companies account for 61 components, or 58.1% of the list. These include, in particular, TMS320F28335PGFA processors for data processing and control of onboard systems, VP230 CAN transceivers for data exchange between modules, MB3238I multichannel transmitters, and PS767D301 voltage regulators. The boards also feature REF3020 reference voltage sources, which provide a stable voltage for measurement circuits.

Militarnyi concluded the report:

With a production rate of 3,000 units per month, this dependence creates a need for more than two million components from Texas Instruments and National Semiconductor combined each year. This indicates a lack of an effective mechanism for monitoring compliance with sanctions, both at the level of the companies themselves and at the government level.

These new findings build on a separate report from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, a US government-funded international news organization, that tore down a Geran-4 drone and found the jet's brain was powered by Texas Instruments chips. They also found many other foreign-made components, much of which came from China.

RFE/RL takes apart a Russian Geran-4 drone to uncover what makes the jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) faster, harder to intercept, and capable of operating deep inside Ukraine -- from its turbojet engine and advanced camera to foreign-made communications and navigation components. @cxemu @radiosvoboda

— Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (@RFERL) September 25, 2026

It remains unclear how and when these chips entered Russia. The recovered chips could have come from inventories stockpiled before sanctions, subsequent purchases through third-country intermediaries or shell companies, or a combination of the two.

The takeaway we have here is how heavily Russia depends on foreign components to power its new one-way attack drone.

title: The Biggest Winners And Losers From The Petrodollar's Decline
desc:
The Biggest Winners And Losers From The Petrodollar's Decline

Authored by Nick Giambruno via InternationalMan.com,

The Iran war is straining US weapons stockpiles and raising doubts about Washington's ability to protect the Persian Gulf.

If that weakens the petrodollar and pushes oil producers away from the US financial system, two assets face clear headwinds: the US dollar and US Treasuries.

The petrodollar system helped create structural demand for both.

If oil exporters sell more energy outside the dollar system, fewer oil dollars need to flow back through Wall Street and into Treasury securities.

At the same time, the US government needs to borrow staggering sums to finance its deficits, military commitments, entitlement programs, and interest expense.

That means rising supply of Treasuries could collide with weakening structural demand.

Watch the 10-year Treasury yield.

The 10-year Treasury yield is perhaps the most important financial benchmark in the global fiat system, as it drives valuations and market trends worldwide. It is widely - and erroneously - regarded as the risk-free rate of return.

The 10-year Treasury yield can be thought of as a key barometer of the US dollar-based fiat system - a critical measure akin to its beating heart.

Bond yields move inversely to bond prices. When bond prices fall, bond yields rise.

A rising 10-year Treasury yield signals trouble for the US dollar because it means investors are selling Treasuries, which pushes up the US government's borrowing costs. That is why the 10-year Treasury yield is a major pain point for the US government.

The 10-year Treasury yield was 3.97% in late February 2026. Now it is around 5.26%, an increase of roughly 129 basis points. 129 bps might not seem like much, but with over $40 trillion in debt and growing, every basis point matters.

At today's debt levels, every 1 basis point increase in the government's average borrowing cost adds roughly $4 billion in annual interest expense. So a 129 bps rise is not trivial - it translates to nearly $516 billion in additional yearly interest costs, materially widening a budget deficit that was already around $1.8 trillion.

I expect the 10-year Treasury yield to keep climbing over the coming weeks and months - until it forces the Fed's hand.

At that point, the intervention will be sold as "stability," but the mechanism will be familiar: suppress yields by debasing the currency.

That feedback loop could become one of the defining investment stories of the years ahead.

The Biggest Winner

The biggest winner should come as no surprise.

Gold.

China and the major Middle Eastern oil producers have accumulated gold for years. I do not think that is a coincidence.

They sit near the center of the changes taking place in the international monetary system.

China produces more gold than any other country and ranks among its largest consumers. Nobody outside Beijing knows how much gold the Chinese state controls, but its official holdings tell only part of the story.

China has also spent years constructing the infrastructure needed to connect yuan-denominated trade with physical gold markets.

That preparation makes much more sense when you view gold not as a commodity, but as a neutral settlement asset.

The last monetary transformation of comparable importance began when Nixon severed the dollar's link to gold in 1971.

Gold traded at $35 per ounce under the old system.

By January 1980, it reached $850 - a gain of more than 2,300%.

I think the monetary shift taking shape today could prove just as important.

For more than half a century, the petrodollar helped create structural demand for dollars and US government debt. It allowed Washington to run deficits and export dollars on a scale no normal country could sustain.

Americans have come to regard that privilege as a permanent feature of the financial landscape.

It isn't.

At first glance, depleted US missile inventories may seem unrelated to the future of the dollar. They aren't. Both depend on the same thing: the ability of the US to convert its enormous financial power into real-world economic and military power.

Washington can create dollars without limit. It cannot create missile factories, rare-earth supply chains, control over the Strait of Hormuz, or confidence in the US security guarantee with a keystroke.

If the Iran war exposes the limits of US military power, pushes the Gulf states toward accommodation with Iran and China, weakens the dollar's role in the oil trade, and accelerates the movement of global reserves toward gold, we could look back on this period as the moment the post-1971 monetary system entered its final stage.

What started with a shortage of missile interceptors leads to a much bigger conclusion: the Iran war is exposing the limits of both American military power and the monetary system that power has supported for more than half a century.

The signals to watch are clear.

Watch the oil producers.

Watch the dollar.

And above all, watch gold.

The petrodollar's decline could push Washington toward more money printing - and put your purchasing power at risk. The time to prepare is before the crisis forces your hand.

For investors, the danger lies in assuming the rules that built yesterday's wealth will protect it tomorrow. A monetary shift of this scale could punish that assumption - and reward those who prepare before the crowd.

title: How I Stopped Worrying, And Learned To Love Data Centers
desc:
How I Stopped Worrying, And Learned To Love Data Centers

Authored by Norm Singleton via RealClearMarkets,

During this time of increased political polarization, it is good to know that there is one issue uniting Trump-loving MAGA Republicans, Bernie Sanders-style Democratic Socialists, and everyone in between: opposition to data centers, especially large data centers built for artificial intelligence (AI). Part of the opposition stems from the public's increasing skepticism of AI. An even larger part is generated by concerns over how AI will drive up electricity costs for those living close to the centers, as well as the high amount of water necessary to run the centers.

Many data center critics ignore the fact that these kinds of facilities have been around for years. As the name suggests, data centers are buildings (or centers) that house the infrastructure and data necessary for the operations of digital services such as the cloud. The typical data center includes servers, switches, routers, and fiber optic cables. These data centers make it possible for individuals to use their phones,and tablets to store and share their photos, messages, and documents, as well as to download and use a wide variety of apps.

While some companies, such as JP Morgan Chase, operate data centers for their own use, other companies operate hyperscalers. These hyperscalers are large enough to host multiple clients. Leading tech firms, including Meta (parent company of Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp), Google, and Amazon Web Services operate hyperscalers that provide services to private companies and government agencies.

Data centers are not just the physical foundation of the internet; they are a source of high-paying jobs. For example, data centers transformed Ashburn, Virginia from a small rural town to a technological hub. The tax revenue generated from the center helped fund improvements in infrastructure, public facilities, and schools. Data centers did not became controversial until the need for larger data centers to accommodate AI led many to blame AI data centers for the increase in electric prices.

Since 2020, residential electric prices have risen by more than 36%. However, studies show that data centers pay a large and growing share of utilities fixed charges, thus reducing costs for other consumers. In addition, tech companies Microsoft and Anthropic have both pledged to pay for any increased electric costs incurred as result of their AI data centers. Other technology companies have signed President Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge to ensure that increased electric costs from AI Data centers are not borne by consumers.

The problem with the electric grid is not that data centers are using too much electricity, but that public utilities failed to invest resources in infrastructure placement during 20 years of flat demand. The increased revenue from AI data centers can help finance the necessary upgrades to the nation's energy grid. AI companies are also exploring uses of alternative energy as a way to reduce costs. Similarly, many AI data centers, including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, are using recycled water to reduce their demand for fresh water. Some technology firms are exploring a way to expand AI data centers without increasing their neighbors' bills by building them in the ocean. Microsoft has already shown that underwater data centers can be just as, if not more, effective than land-based ones.

According to University of North Carolina Management Professor Nir Kshetri:

"In 2015, Microsoft launched a research project to explore the feasibility, benefits and challenges of underwater data centers." Part of that effort included setting up a waterproof data center on the seafloor near Scotland's Orkney Islands in 2018. It contained 864 servers and was connected to shore by an underwater cable.

"After two years, Microsoft reported that the servers in the underwater data center failed at about one-eighth the rate of servers in comparable land-based data centers. The company is still studying the possible reasons but hypothesizes that in a sealed underwater environment the equipment is less exposed to oxygen, humidity, and temperature fluctuations - as well as less jostling from people working to replace broken components."

Unfortunately, despite their initial success, Microsoft has suspended its underwater data centers when they ended the experiment in 2024. Hopefully, Microsoft or another tech company will take up underwater data center development and/or discover other ways to meet the need for AI data centers without increasing other Americans' electric bills. Tech companies can do this as long as government limits its role to ensuring that companies compensate Americans for any harms caused by their operations.

title: 5 Challenges Facing South America's Copper Boom
desc:
5 Challenges Facing South America's Copper Boom

Authored by Charles Kennedy via OilPrice.com,

  • Escondida supervisors, about 1,020 workers at the world’s largest copper mine, said they would strike at 8 a.m. local time Wednesday, a week after workers walked out at Centinela.

  • Chile’s August copper output fell 12.8% to 369,500 tons, the lowest monthly total since February 2011, and a fatal landslide hit Codelco’s El Teniente on Sunday.

  • The IEA still sees primary copper supply about 25% short of requirements by 2035, while Peru targets $33 billion in mining investment and Argentina’s Vicuña aims for a final investment decision by year-end.

Supervisors at BHP's Escondida, the world's largest copper mine, said they would strike at 8 a.m. local time Wednesday after government-led mediation failed to produce a contract. The union represents about 1,020 workers at a mine that supplies roughly a quarter of Chile's copper, and the stoppage follows a walkout at Antofagasta's Centinela that began Oct. 7. Both land as governments across the Andes ask miners for far more copper, not less.

Demand will not wait

S&P Global projects that copper demand will climb from 28 million metric tons in 2025 to 42 million tons by 2040, with AI data centers and defense each roughly tripling their consumption, and it warns that supply could fall 10 million tons short. The IEA still sees primary supply about 25% short of requirements in 2035, down from a 30% gap in last year's edition.

Copper runs through grids, electric vehicles, wind and solar farms and the AI data center buildout, which S&P says could account for 14% of U.S. power demand by 2030, so a shortfall in the metal reaches well beyond mining. BloombergNEF has warned that a tight market could bring cost inflation or delays for electrification projects. Peru is targeting at least $33 billion in mining investment over five years, and Chile's pipeline tops $100 billion over the decade.

Chile keeps losing output

Chile's copper output fell 12.8% in August from a year earlier to 369,500 tons, the lowest monthly figure since February 2011, according to national statistics data reported by Bloomberg. On Sunday, heavy rain triggered a landslide at Codelco's El Teniente mine that killed two contractors and led the company to partially suspend operations, and El Niño could bring more rain to Chile and Peru in the months ahead.

Cochilco expects national production to fall 2.6% this year to 5.27 million tons before recovering to 5.55 million in 2027. TD Securities analysts said strike votes, worker fatalities and operational disruptions have helped "maintain a supply-risk premium," and copper has held close to its September record high.

China's acid squeeze

Morgan Stanley estimated in April that 1.1 million tons of Chile's annual leached copper output, more than half its refined production, could be exposed to a Chinese ban on sulphuric acid exports. Miners use the acid to leach metal from ore, and Chinese customs data showed shipments to Chile fell to zero in March, with Beijing reportedly planning a full halt from May.

Permits and protests

Permitting in Chile can take as long as 12 years in some cases, according to GlobalData, and President José Antonio Kast ordered ministers in March to clear 50 pending claims tied to about $16 billion in projects. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori's government wants to authorize 240 exploration and extraction projects this year, yet the Observatory of Mining Conflicts counts nearly 200 social conflicts nationwide, 64 of them tied to mining and other environmental disputes, and says most of the main mining regions voted against her.

Argentina starts from zero

Argentina has not produced copper since the Alumbrera mine closed in 2018, which makes Vicuña, the BHP and Lundin Mining venture, its biggest test. The project received the top tier of RIGI benefits this year, and its backers are targeting a final investment decision on a $7.1 billion first phase before year-end, with first copper planned for 2030.

In April, a judge in neighboring La Rioja ordered a 30-day suspension and blocked machinery from using an access road through the province, saying the province had been left out of the environmental assessment. A San Juan court allowed work to continue days later.

title: Susie Wiles Reportedly Orchestrated Zacharia's Firing With Hannity Hit
desc:
Susie Wiles Reportedly Orchestrated Zacharia's Firing With Hannity Hit

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who did not favor Katie Zacharia for press secretary, helped line up the Fox News interview that ultimately led to Zacharia's being fired from the job, according to two people familiar with internal West Wing dynamics who spoke with Politico.

One source described the appearance as a "sanctioned hit" on Zacharia. The second person said, "[White House spokesperson] Danielle [Alvarez] and Susie fed her to Hannity," and noted that Wiles and Hannity are friendly and speak often. One source said Zacharia had not been Wiles' preferred choice for press secretary.

The account comes as Wiles faces questions about her own standing with the president. As Republicans' midterm prospects worsen, Trump has asked allies about Wiles and floated possible replacements, but the White House denies those reports.

Hannity opened the interview by addressing Zacharia's first press briefing, which ran 14 minutes and included three questions. "It's been widely panned. I'm sure you're aware," Hannity said.

Zacharia responded by laying out a compressed timeline. She said she received the offer by phone the previous Wednesday, flew to Washington for a Friday meeting, went home to California on Saturday, and returned Sunday. She said she started on Monday, the Columbus Day federal holiday, and received briefing materials on the morning of her Tuesday briefing.

"So what I feel is I really stepped up to the plate to do the press conference, shaken, with very little prep time," she said.

Hannity asked whether she believed staff should have prepared her better. Zacharia said she could have limited the session to a brief introduction. "Instead of taking questions, probably should have stepped aside," she said.

Hannity then asked whether she had failed the bar exam. "Yes, Sean," Zacharia said. She told Hannity she had preregistered for the exam before moving to China after graduating from Pepperdine, and that she later worked in the international practice of a Chinese law firm. Asked whether she ever retook the exam, she said, "No, I did not."

Hannity cited a report identifying 15 social media posts in which Zacharia described herself as an attorney. "I think they were retweets," Zacharia said. "I corrected the record and said it's not endorsing the title."

"And why not say, 'I took the bar and didn't pass it'?" Hannity asked. Zacharia said she had four children in six years after returning to the United States and never intended to practice law. She said she held a valid Juris Doctor and offered general legal commentary in media appearances without giving legal advice.

Watch video

Zacharia's performance in the interview drew widespread criticism on social media, and Trump told reporters the next day that he asked Zacharia to consider whether she wanted to stay in the role. "She was on Sean Hannity last night. And Sean was a little bit tough. I saw she was on Fox and Friends this morning. They were a little tough," Trump said.

Trump said he told Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want to."

But the White House rejects the claim that Wiles orchestrated Zacharia's downfall. "Susie and Sean do talk, but Susie did not need to feed her to Sean or anybody else. It's not her style," a senior White House official said.

The same official pointed to Zacharia's own media appearances, including a Friday morning interview on Fox & Friends. "And Hannity wasn't the nail in her coffin; her hit [on Fox & Friends] this morning was, as well as her weird answer on being a lawyer," the official said.

Watch video

White House communications director Steven Cheung dismissed the reports of Wiles' involvement. "All of this breathless speculation is just that - speculation. And it's fiction that's not even creative," Cheung said. He added that Zacharia "will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role." Zacharia declined to comment.

Fox News Media insists that Hannity alone decides whom he interviews and what he asks, and that "Wiles and Alvarez had nothing to do with the booking." A Fox News insider also rejected the idea of a planned hit. "If you can't answer simple questions about your credentials, that speaks volumes," the insider said.

The credentials questions began three days before the Hannity interview, when a reporter shouted a question at a White House departure. "You said she's an attorney. Where did she pass the bar exam?" the reporter asked. Zacharia answered "when I moved to China." She later admitted she failed the California bar exam in 2011 and never took it again.

"Not only is Fox News home turf for us, but Katie couldn't manage to answer a basic question about herself that had been brewing in the news for three days," a pro-Trump operative told Politico.

The press secretary job marked Zacharia's second short tenure in the administration. Earlier this year, she spent less than two months at the Department of Homeland Security.

title: California Should Not Get To Set Policy For All Of The US
desc:
California Should Not Get To Set Policy For All Of The US

Authored by Curtis Hill via RealClearMarkets,

California has decided it should dictate how the rest of America packages everything from cereal and soap to industrial spare parts.

Seventeen Republican attorneys general have filed suit to stop it. They are right. The rest of the country should say so - and reject California's attempt to impose its policies on everyone else.

California's Senate Bill 54 effectively tells companies: If you want to sell in California, redesign your packaging, cut plastic on California's timetable, and pay fees to a private Washington, D.C., organization called Circular Action Alliance. CAA sets the fees, keeps its methodology confidential, and handles disputes through arbitration rather than a court.

But packaging is not a California issue. It is a national supply-chain issue. Companies do not invent a unique box for Sacramento and another for South Bend. They build one system. When California attaches conditions to its market, those conditions travel. Costs travel with them - onto manufacturers, distributors, and the families who buy toothpaste and canned goods in states that never voted for this scheme.

California is using the size of its market to impose its preferences on commerce that happens everywhere else. The attorneys general call that what it is: one state trying to set national policy.

I have seen this movie before.

As Indiana Attorney General, I led multistate efforts against this same tactic. California cities tried to use "public nuisance" lawsuits to dictate national energy policy from a courtroom in San Francisco. I argued then that California localities cannot regulate economic activity beyond their borders, and that the nation should not sit idle while California tried to turn itself into a regulatory empire.

We also led a coalition to the U.S. Supreme Court challenging Massachusetts's attempt to tell farmers in other states how to house their hens and hogs as a condition of selling eggs and pork in Boston. Same theory. Same abuse. Market access as a weapon.

California and a handful of like-minded states have a playbook: Pass a rule at home. Make compliance a condition of doing business. Watch national supply chains conform because it is cheaper to surrender than to maintain two systems. Then call the result "progress" and dare anyone to object.

That is not federalism. It is the big dog sitting on the porch, growling at every other house on the street.

Multistate action is how the other states push back. One attorney general filing a brief is a protest. Seventeen states joining a federal lawsuit - alongside a business that has already challenged this model in Oregon - send a message a judge must take seriously.

This is not a trade association seeking a special exemption. It is sovereign states defending their authority to set policy for their own people. And it tells Sacramento that when California exports the costs of its policies, the response will be coordinated legal action - not a press release and a shrug.

That is the point of the office I once held. An attorney general is not a commentator; the job is to defend the state's legal interests when another government tries to impose its policies beyond its borders. California's packaging scheme does exactly that. Fees collected by a private organization with little meaningful public oversight are one back door. So is a mandate that forces a plant in Iowa or a distributor in Indiana to pay for California's regulatory experiment.

None of this requires opposition to clean streets, recycling, or reducing waste. States are free to run recycling programs, set their own environmental policies, and punish fraud or deception in labeling. What they may not do is force businesses across the country to follow one state's rules while handing the collection plate to an unelected private organization. States can pursue their own policies. They cannot conscript the interstate economy into a single regulatory religion.

The seventeen attorneys general are doing the unglamorous work of saying no. They deserve support - from other states, from boards that still remember fiduciary duty, and from anyone who understands that the Constitution divided power for a reason. California is large. It is not the legislature of the United States.

If other states sit this one out, they should not be surprised when the next California rule arrives already attached to their store shelves. Empires are not always built with armies. Sometimes they are built with a market, a mandate, and a fee.

Curtis Hill is Senior Fellow with the Free Enterprise Project and former Indiana Attorney General.

title: Oregon School Gunman's Shotgun Was Bought By His Mother: Sources
desc:
Oregon School Gunman's Shotgun Was Bought By His Mother: Sources

Police in Bend, Oregon, say they are still working out how a 16-year-old got the shotgun he used to kill three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary, even as multiple outlets, citing unnamed officials, say that his mother bought it.

The shooter, identified by Police Chief Mike Krantz as Griffin J. John II, walked up to the school's fence at 12:58 p.m. Thursday, threw the weapon over it and climbed after it. A pickup driver who confronted him made the first 911 call; he fired at the truck, hitting it at least three times, and the driver was unhurt. He then shot out the glass in the school's locked doors and went into the special needs classroom just inside, where he fired "as many as 15 rounds," Krantz said. Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher were killed. A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old staff member were wounded.

Every victim was shot in the special needs classroom of the school John once attended, where he had been a special needs student, according to Superintendent Steven Cook and the police chief. "All of the victims were shot in that classroom," Krantz said, per CBS. No motive has been given; Krantz told reporters, "we may never get that full answer, but we want it."

The gun was a Maverick 88, a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, which Krantz said was found near him with a backpack. John fired birdshot, buckshot and slugs, and ABC reports another 44 rounds were recovered from him and his backpack.

Police have not confirmed on the record that the mother bought the gun. NBC says multiple officials told it she bought the shotgun around his August birthday, and two law enforcement officials told it she has been cooperative. CBS and ABC cite sources too, and ABC says officials haven't confirmed it. The Bend Source reports that police declined to say whether the parents were cooperating or to confirm the purchase. Investigators have searched the family's home under a warrant. No charges against anyone have been reported. Our earlier post carried an Associated Press source's claim that the purchase was legal; nothing police have said on the record establishes that.

Oregon law is permissive on the purchase itself. A person must be 18 to buy a rifle or shotgun, NBC notes, and ORS 166.470 bars transferring a firearm to anyone under 18, but exempts a parent, or someone with a parent's consent, handing a minor a firearm other than a handgun, as well as temporary transfers for hunting, target practice or another lawful purpose. A violation is a Class A misdemeanor. A mother buying a shotgun and giving it to her son would not, on those facts alone, fall under the ban.

The storage rules are the harder test. Oregon's 2021 gun law, SB 554, requires firearms to be secured with a trigger or cable lock, in a locked container or in a gun room. The Giffords Law Center, a gun-control group, summarizes the rest: owners must secure a gun whenever it is not carried or controlled by an authorized person, penalties rise if a minor gets an unsecured firearm, and whoever transfers a firearm to a minor must directly supervise its use, with failure counted as negligence per se in a civil suit.

The facts that decide it are not public: where the gun was kept, who held the key, whether anyone supervised him. Investigators are going through his computer, phone, social media and search history, CBS reports, including whether he was fixated on earlier mass shootings; sources stressed the inquiry is preliminary. Police have asked the public for video from Oct. 15 around Third Street and Brosterhous Road, and the Bend Source says the scene is expected to be released Oct. 20.

A bystander ended the attack. Kaylub Giamanco, 36, a carpenter with two daughters at the school and a concealed-weapon permit, according to his brother, followed the shooter in with a .40-caliber pistol that Krantz said he had "legally secured in his vehicle," saw a teacher struggling with the gunman, and fired, "striking the suspect multiple times."

title: Wall Street Converges On Almonty Investor Day As Pentagon's Tungsten Clock Ticks Down
desc:
Wall Street Converges On Almonty Investor Day As Pentagon's Tungsten Clock Ticks Down

We have highlighted "owning the bottlenecks" as one of our core themes (aside from nuclear, AI, etc.) as China tightens control over critical materials and the West races to secure conflict-free supplies ahead of a rearmament supercycle. Miners with operating assets and near-term delivery capacity are best positioned to capture the next leg of the cycle, as Western governments seek reliable and conflict-free supplies.

Mining equities have largely de-rated since their May peak, retracing the massive gains made in early 2025, when Beijing's restrictions on tungsten, germanium, gallium, and other defense-critical materials helped spark the rally. We view the pullback as a correction within a broader structural bull market, with the next phase likely to reward miners capable of converting ore into finished critical materials that meet the coming surge in demand from the defense industry.

We view tungsten, a defense-critical metal, as one of the most critical metals needed for the rearmament supercycle because of its high density, heat resistance, and performance in wear-resistant materials. This metal is commonly found in armor-piercing ammunition, missiles, interceptors, fighter jets, and bombers, and the list of defense applications is endless.

Ahead of Almonty Industries' Investor Day on Monday, Wall Street's mining and metals desks have been focused on the company's position as a leading Western-aligned supplier of conflict-free tungsten outside China. Analysts from Oppenheimer, D.A. Davidson, Cantor Fitzgerald, Stifel, Jefferies, and other firms are expected to attend.

With a supply agreement already locked with Pennsylvania-based Global Tungsten & Powders and its South Korean Sangdong mining operations ramping up, Almonty is positioned to benefit from rising demand for defense-grade tungsten as missile and bomb production expands.

Oppenheimer special situations analyst Ian Zaffino wrote on Thursday that, despite tungsten/APT prices moderating from $3,140 per MTU to $2,700 per MTU in the most recent week, "management believes upstream availability of concentrate remains tight, and should remain so, as US defense restrictions go into effect January 1, 2027."

Zaffino is referring to tighter U.S. defense procurement restrictions on tungsten scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027. The requirements will soon extend beyond melting and manufacturing to include mining, refining, and separation, restricting covered tungsten products sourced through China, Russia, and other designated countries.

For example, processing Chinese- or Russian-origin tungsten in a third country would not, by itself, establish the needed compliance. This shift could strengthen Almonty's competitive position as its Sangdong operation ramps into Phase 2 production.

"Sangdong continues to ramp with its first shipment expected in late-October. This is slightly behind our initial assumptions and we therefore adjust our 3Q26E/4Q26E revenue/EBITDA," Zaffino said.

He noted that Almonty "has cash of ~$865M (net cash of ~$290M), which should fund projects including Sangdong Phase 2 and the oxide facility, as well as share buybacks."

Even though Zaffino lowered his 12-month price target from $25 to $19, reflecting lower peer multiples amid the selloff in mining stocks over the last several months, he said, "We believe shares are attractive (5.7x/4.2x FY27E/FY28E EBITDA), particularly as Sangdong ramps and supply remains tight."

Ahead of Investor Day on Monday, Zaffino outlined five key points:

The Sangdong processing plant received final certification (on 9/17) and is now able to produce concentrate. Grinding is at full throughput, and the company continues to optimize the flotation process. This should put Sangdong on pace to commence shipments in late October. We expect Sangdong Phase 1 to deliver ~640K tons of ore annually (or ~240K MTU of concentrate), worth ~$500M of revenues at current prices.

Outside of Sangdong, ALM has announced several projects to bring tungsten to market. In Rwanda, ALM will acquire, upgrade, and export existing ore, pre-concentrate, and tailings, with exports commencing in November. At Los Santos (Spain), ALM entered into a multi-year offtake agreement for the recycling of the existing tailings stockpile. The Montana/Gentung-Browns project represents longer-term optionality for US supply with "slow-and-steady" development.

While tungsten prices have moderated somewhat from their highs, supply fundamentals remain supportive. Tungsten/APT is $2,700/MTU, vs. ~$3,000/MTU from July through September. Western APT/oxide plants are operating at capacity under long-term contracts, which has limited their ability to absorb additional concentrate. As a result, concentrate prices have softened, even as availability of finished APT/oxide in the West remains constrained.

The company will host an investor day on 10/19. We anticipate an overview of the tungsten market and pricing, and operational updates across the portfolio. ALM should report 3Q26 results in mid-November. For 3Q, we now estimate revenue/EBITDA of C$49M/$25M (vs. C$75M/$47M previously), vs. the Street's C$94M/$66M. We forecast revenue/EBITDA increases to C$75M/$57M in 4Q26 (vs. C$110M/$99M previously), as Sangdong ramps towards full Phase 1.

Overall, ALM is set to start shipments from South Korea in late October and is well positioned with additional supply/offtake arrangements. Tungsten fundamentals remain healthy, and we anticipate supply will remain tight ahead of US defense procurement rules that cover recycled material as well. We believe catalysts remain, including the investor day, Sangdong's shipments, buybacks, and the ramp of Phase 2 at Sangdong.

Below are Zaffino's updated base-case assumptions, upside and downside scenarios, and upcoming catalysts:

Separately, Bank of America metals and mining analyst Lawson Winder wrote on Thursday that Monday's Investor Day in New York could provide greater clarity on tungsten market conditions and execution of Sangdong's Phase 2 expansion:

  • Tungsten market fundamentals: Management commentary on the sustainability of current tungsten pricing, long-term incentive pricing, the evolution of contract structures (including price floors), the durability of the current defense demand cycle, customer negotiations, and spot vs. contract exposure.
  • Sangdong Phase 1 ramp-up: We see Q3'26 primarily as a re-risking quarter for ALM, as it ramps up Phase 1 of its new Sangdong tungsten mine in Korea. On 23-Sep-26, ALM announced first production for Sangdong Phase 1. On 29-Sep-28, CEO Lewis Black said the mill was operating 13 hours per day / 7 days per week, and it would move to 24-hour days / 7 days per week "over the coming days." We expect the market to watch for a clear statement that the mine is operating continuously, with a timeline to nameplate capacity (around 1,100 tonnes per day (tpd)).
  • Sangdong Phase 2 expansion: Update on engineering work, capital requirements, underground development milestones, and key gating factors to increase processing capacity to roughly 1.2m tpa and double concentrate production.
  • Sangdong molybdenum project: Progress of the 12,000-meter drilling program and the timeline for the announcement of updated reserves and resources.
  • Gentung Browns Lake (Montana): Current permitting and development status at Browns Lake. Potential for funding support and/or an offtake agreement from the U.S. Department of War (DoW).
  • Note that ALM is scheduled to host an investor day in New York on Monday, October 19. Many of these issues and more could also be addressed there, in advance of the Q3'26 results release.

desc:
Clancy Contagion Spreads: Queens Mom Kills Her Kindergartener

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

A 5-year-old about to start school is dead after her mother called 911 and said "I killed my daughter," in what some are calling yet another Lindsay Clancy copycat killing.

In a South Richmond Hill home in Queens, police found 5-year-old Fabiana Cabello unconscious, bleeding from her nose and mouth with a bruise on her temple. Her mother, 32-year-old Francis Cabello, had called 911 just before 7 p.m. on Wednesday, admitting to killing her own child.

Officers rushed Fabiana to Jamaica Hospital. She did not survive. Autopsy findings showed scrapes and broken blood vessels around her eyes, heart, and lungs consistent with asphyxia. Cabello was charged with second-degree murder and held without bail.

🚨 HORRIFIC: A 5-year-old girl in Queens was killed, and police say her own mother confessed to the crime. Little Fabiana was about to start kindergarten. Pure evil. Pray for this family and demand justice for this innocent sweet girl! 💔🙏🏻 https://t.co/mVNqoBVFwX

— Ryan Fournier (@RyanAFournier) October 17, 2026

Her father told reporters she had psychological issues, had recently stopped taking medication, and had been hospitalized months earlier.

He said, "I was paying attention because she was already acting strange. I knew that she stopped taking the medication. ... She said the doctor authorized her to stop taking the medicine." He added, "We hope the judge takes into consideration her mental health."

This is the latest case in a documented cluster that accelerated with the trial of Lindsay Clancy who admits to having strangled her three children in Duxbury, Massachusetts, in January 2023.

At this point it seems to have become an epidemic of horror.

One X user who has been tracking local reports since the Clancy case listed 82 mothers who killed 123 of their own children, with 37 more attempts in which 52 children survived.

Since Lindsay Clancy: 82 mothers have killed 123 of their own children. 37 MORE mothers tried. 52 children survived. These are just the ones that made the local news. Every time, the same excuse: Postpartum. Hormones. Psychosis. NO. Hormones are not a defense and the mothers are not the victims. The children are. The moment we call the killer a victim, the children never get justice. Someone has to speak for them. So I will. America, we have a problem.

— 🏴‍☠️LibertysBelle 🇺🇸 (@Libertys_Belle) October 16, 2026

The update after the Queens death brought the tally to 83 mothers and 124 children. The numbers cover only cases that reached local news.

The recurring frame is identical: postpartum depression, hormones, psychosis, medication. The children are treated as collateral damage to the mother's crisis.

Clancy's own case remains unresolved. A jury deadlocked 11-1 in favor of finding her not criminally responsible after seven days of deliberations in early September.

The holdout, Michael Desronvil, has since given his first televised interview. He told Kayleigh McEnany he had no reasonable doubt, describing Clancy's actions as methodical and stating, "What I would like the world to know about me is that I do extremely care about people, especially children, because children are extremely innocent."

He has reported media swarming his home, including footage of people going through his mail and peering in windows. Other jurors have publicly described him as hostile and unwilling to apply the legal standard.

On October 1, Judge William Sullivan denied the defense motion for a required finding of not guilty, writing that the prosecution's evidence "was sufficient to satisfy any rational trier of fact beyond a reasonable doubt" on both the killings and criminal responsibility.

The next hearing is set for November 2, where the parties will address double-jeopardy arguments, a defense request for further inquiry into the holdout juror, and a possible retrial date.

Clancy's separate medical malpractice suit against Women & Infants Hospital of Rhode Island and other providers is also advancing; the hospital has filed responses raising comparative negligence and informed consent defenses.

The cultural response to Clancy has been the through-line. Women gathered outside the Plymouth courthouse in pink, holding signs and telling reporters they understood how she could have killed her children.

Online, mothers posted videos with their own infants under captions such as "Same, Lindsay." A GoFundMe for Clancy's parents raised more than a million dollars.

Conspiracy theories shifted blame onto her husband.

The holdout juror and his family faced harassment and stalking once his identity circulated. Supporters threatened the father of the children Clancy killed.

Commentators including Joe Rogan and Bill Maher publicly questioned why a woman who strangled three toddlers had fans.

An Illinois case involving Corie Walsh drew similar attention after she was charged with killing her 2-year-old son. Prosecutors noted she had been texting about the Clancy trial hours earlier.

Whether or not any single subsequent case is a direct imitation, the volume of mothers killing their children and the speed with which mental-health framing appears as the primary story both rose after Clancy's trial became a social-media event.

When the killer is immediately recast as the principal victim, the dead children disappear from the narrative.

Fabiana Cabello was five years old and preparing for kindergarten. Cora, Dawson, and Callan Clancy were five, three, and eight months. The pattern of treating the mothers as the story and the children as the symptom continues.

Justice for the dead requires rejecting the idea that hormones erase responsibility. The children are the victims. Someone still has to say so.

title: The NRC Lost A Sixth Of Its Staff... So Why Are Reactor Reviews Getting Faster?
desc:
The NRC Lost A Sixth Of Its Staff... So Why Are Reactor Reviews Getting Faster?

For the past year, critics have warned that DOGE gutted the Nuclear Regulatory Commission just as the nuclear renaissance was getting started.

If the president really wants to kickstart the "nuclear renaissance," gutting the NRC of its expertise and rubber-stamping projects isn't the way to go. It will only slow processes down, increase the potential for accidents, and erode public trust.

— Josh Freed (@jsfreed) July 30, 2025

The NRC's headcount fell more than 16% between July 2024 and June 2026, from 2,957 to 2,477, according to a new GAO report. About 740 people left, only 270 were hired, and attrition hit 12.4% in FY2025, up from 7.6% a year earlier.

But the GAO never says the agency is broken. Instead, their report says "most stakeholders and NRC officials told us they were not concerned about NRC's ability to ensure safety or the timely review of applications."

Some have also characterized the staffing reduction as a purge. The GAO report objectively contradicts that claim, as the NRC let go of just four, and nine in ten departures were retirements or resignations.

Hiring stalled under a federal freeze, but by this recent spring new hires outnumbered departures again.

"The NRC did not lose its way or the ability to perform its mission," Commissioner David Wright, who chaired the agency through the exodus, said in March. "Instead, everyone stepped up."

Would keeping them have even mattered?

What the GAO is unable to prove is that the NRC would be ready for the coming wave of applications if all those people had stayed.

History suggests it wouldn't be. When the GAO sounded a similar alarm in 2007, the NRC was bracing for "at least 20 applications for 29 new nuclear power reactors." It staffed up to about 4,000 employees by 2010, still took nearly four years to license Vogtle 3 and 4, and watched most of the other applications fizzle.

In other words, the NRC shed roughly 1,000 people in the 14 years before anyone had heard of DOGE.

"In the last renaissance, the NRC hired a lot of people for what they anticipated in new reactor licensing applications," Chairman Ho Nieh told House lawmakers in April. This time, "instead of just hiring people to handle the work, we are fundamentally looking at how we make these decisions."

What the GAO didn't weigh

The report also doesn't test whether that streamlining has made up for the people the NRC lost.

It's "too soon to assess," the GAO says, and it skips the math of how many applications are coming, how many hours each takes under the new rules, and how many qualified reviewers that requires.

NRC officials told the GAO that new efficiency measures could cut the agency's staffing needs by about 300 full-time positions. That's more than half of what it lost on net.

Asked about staffing at a May Senate hearing, Doug Weaver, the newest commissioner, said the NRC is "not simply doing the same old way of doing our work and trying to do it faster with fewer people. We're fundamentally changing the way we do licensing."

And it's already showing. Late last month, the NRC approved construction of the first BWRX-300 small modular reactor in 14 months. "Four months ahead of schedule is what the new NRC looks like," Nieh said.

But Chairman Nieh is still missing the bulk of the celebration. Back when the NRC was looking at a significantly larger staff, the estimated timeline was 36 months to hear back for the same license. Today, they have less staff and finished 22 months faster.

The DOGE operative

Seth Cohen, the ex-Kirkland & Ellis lawyer who came to the NRC with DOGE and later became the Energy Department's chief counsel for nuclear policy, sat on the steering committee overseeing that rewrite. ProPublica’s Avi Asher-Schapiro made him the face of the "DOGE Goes Nuclear" piece.

Yet Cohen told an American Nuclear Society conference last November that "the NRC is almost certainly going to be growing in the coming years," and denied the goal was to "make this the tiniest Nuclear Regulatory Commission it can be."

When he left government in June, Asher-Schapiro labeled Cohen "one of the key figures reshaping the regulatory environment to benefit Silicon Valley-backed advanced reactor firms."

Cohen's reply? “Get bent, soyboy”

Now that I’m out of government, I can finally respond for myself: Get bent, soyboy. We didn’t do this for “Silicon Valley . . . companies.” We did this for you, for your family, your community, your state, your nation, and your species. Nuclear energy provides the safest, highest density, reliable power available on our planet. My career colleagues at DOE and NRC inspired me to think about nuclear as a way to forge American steel and electrolyze aluminum without releasing particulate matter, to desalinate water in the Middle East and save humanity from resource wars. By rejecting the false narratives and Cold War hysteria, we can secure the next American century while raising whole countries out of poverty. Do you really think I left an incredible career at Kirkland, paid out of pocket for an apartment in DC and dozens of cross-country trips, and left my family on the west coast because I wanted to enrich people I never met before taking this job? I came to D.C. to do something that mattered, to satisfy a driving curiosity (more on that later), and, most importantly, to serve. As I learned more about nuclear energy and its history, I developed a conviction that one nuclear’s biggest issues was a culture of cynicism: nothing new or exciting could happen because it would end in disappointment, and that militated against rocking the boat even a tiny bit. The career staff in government and their industry counterparts lived through dark winters before and stopped believing that warm springs could bloom into summers. I have two core philosophies. First, I believe in ruthless optimism. Rational decision making requires detached risk analysis. But we also cannot win if we believe we can lose. Merging the two requires orienting teams around driving missions. That way, when a real opportunity presents itself, you can take a huge swing. If I take credit for anything—honestly, almost all of the success belongs to the incredible and dedicated people at @ENERGY and @NRCgov—it’s countering the cultural rot and morass that risked forfeiting American excellence. My colleagues and I gave cover to the scientists and engineers, which freed them up to focus on delivering safe power. And, as success materialized, they started to dream again. That’s why the pilot program succeeded, and why I feel confident about the future of NLICs and NRC reform. Nobody needs me anymore because they can innovate on their own. My second core philosophy is to assume positive intent. Avi, I know that you heard about my real motivations from multiple people you interviewed when preparing your hit piece on me. Rather than telling that story, one which could help inspire another generation of people to use their talents for the greater good, you ignored them. Instead, you implied that Peter Thiel recruited me for nefarious purposes. (I’ve never met him, but, @peterthiel, if you’re reading this, I’m a huge fan!) Nuclear regulation starts and ends with safety. I promised everyone I worked with that I would resign before doing or pushing for anything that could compromise public safety. But I also distinguished between real safety and performative bullshit. That’s what the careers came to embrace, too. We love nuclear, why would we do anything that could risk threatening its future? America faces a crossroads. We can either trod a road of cultural decay or hike our way back to the peak of global innovation. Join me on the latter path. Correct the fear mongering and conspiracies and tell the story of America’s great reindustrialization. Tell the story of our public servants, our great entrepreneurs, our scientific dominance. Tell the real story about how DOGE went nuclear.

— Seth Cohen (@OverReactor1776) June 20, 2026

The real competition

Cohen himself now sits on the board of fuel maker Standard Nuclear, which points to the NRC's real staffing problem.

The agency has always lost people to industry, but never to this many well-funded startups at once. Investors have poured $4.6 billion into U.S. nuclear startups this year, as we noted last week, and half the stakeholders the GAO interviewed had hired former NRC staff.

"They're hiring people from the NRC and they're paying them far more than the federal government pays," Nieh said in June.

The NRC hasn't fought back much on pay. Of the hiring, pay and bonus tools Congress handed it in the ADVANCE Act, it has used only 18 performance bonuses worth $335,000 combined. Officials told the GAO that targeted raises would be hard to justify without raising pay across whole job series, which would likely mean higher fees for applicants.

The GAO's fix? Finish a workforce planning tool that has already missed two target dates, and set metrics for whether the NRC's hiring tools are enough.

title: Egypt's Sisi Declares His Presidency Will End In 2030
desc:
Egypt's Sisi Declares His Presidency Will End In 2030

Via Middle East Eye

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has declared that his presidential term will end in 2030 and that the question of his departure from office is now "settled and will not be discussed".

Sisi, 71, said on Saturday during a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy that "the Egyptian constitution would not be touched". He is currently serving a six-year term.

"The year 2030 will mark the end of my presidential term. This matter is completely settled," Sisi said.

"I will not leave the Egyptian state until it is brimming with its own people capable of shouldering responsibility."

The president added that the military academy was creating a new generation of leaders.

Sisi came to power in 2013 after leading a military coup that deposed Egypt’s first democratically elected president, Mohamed Morsi.

Rights groups estimate that over 60,000 prisoners of conscience are held in Egyptian jails, including more than 1,000 women.

Many prisoners, including former President Morsi and several opposition figures, have died as a result of medical neglect and other inhumane prison conditions, according to rights groups.

Sisi's latest comments come at a turbulent time in the region. Last week, Egypt’s foreign minister reaffirmed the country's support for Saudi Arabia in its conflict with Yemen's Houthis, saying that "Gulf security is integral to Egypt’s national security and our solidarity with Saudi Arabia."

Egypt has also been involved in military conflict with its neighbors. Last week, an Egyptian air strike killed 72 civilian workers at a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border.

Egypt backs the Sudanese Armed Forces in its war against the UAE-backed paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

Egyptian President el-Sisi on leaving office by 2030: I’m saying this more than 40 months in advance so that no one can claim I’m preparing someone from my family or relatives to take over. No, no, no. Nothing like that. This is a very big country, and such things cannot happen here.

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 17, 2026

Sisi's government is also at loggerheads with Ethiopia, which it sees as a potential naval rival in the Red Sea and with which it has a long-standing dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.

Egypt recently hosted a conference with representatives from Sudan, Somalia and Eritrea to discuss coordinating military and intelligence efforts should conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea escalate.

title: Nurse Deemed 'Not Disabled Enough' For Payout After COVID Jab Paralysis
desc:
Nurse Deemed 'Not Disabled Enough' For Payout After COVID Jab Paralysis

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

An NHS nurse in the UK has been denied compensation despite being permanently damaged by a COVID vaccine during a trial.

Marie-Claire Hoyle, who volunteered for the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine trial in 2020 developed transverse myelitis two weeks after her second dose, temporarily shutting down the global trial.

The qualified advanced nurse practitioner and NHS England's network manager for high-consequence infectious diseases, lost the use of her hands, became numb from collarbone to thigh, and still carries permanent spinal cord damage visible on MRI. The Vaccine Damage Payment Scheme acknowledged the vaccine caused her condition yet refused the £120,000 one-off payment because her disability improved below the rigid 60% lifelong threshold.

Nurse struck by rare condition linked to Covid vaccine 'not disabled enough' for compensation https://t.co/wuobqdFmB0

— GB News (@GBNEWS) October 16, 2026

Hoyle that's related how she was on shift when pain hit her neck and spine, spreading within an hour into her shoulders and hands. "I lost the ability to use my hands, I couldn't hold a pen, I couldn't hold a toothbrush. I was completely numb from my collarbone down to my thigh level because the signals from my spine and brain had been damaged."

An MRI confirmed transverse myelitis. The trial paused worldwide while her case was assessed; she survived and recovered enough for it to resume. Permanent damage remains. "I've had an MRI since and there is still damage in my spinal cord, which will never heal. I have really poor grip in my fingertips, so I constantly drop things. I still have nerve pain down the left side of my arm and numbness across my central chest and that will never resolve," she further stated.

She received a high five-figure out-of-court settlement from Oxford University. The VDPS, however, ruled she no longer qualified. "They acknowledged that the vaccine caused my transverse myelitis, based on the evidence I supplied with all my medical records, and at the time I was seriously harmed on a value of up to 60%. However, they said: 'You aren't now, so you don't need the payment.'"

Hoyle, a mother of three who later had her youngest vaccinated and says she continues to support vaccines in principle, wants a scalable system matching actual ongoing harm rather than an all-or-nothing cutoff.

AstraZeneca later withdrew its Vaxzevria vaccine worldwide in 2024, officially citing commercial reasons and the shift to updated formulations. The company had already admitted in court documents that the shot can cause thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome. Kate Scott, whose husband was left with permanent brain injury, said the decision looked less commercial and more like recognition that the product no longer sat "within the acceptable safety parameters," given 445 confirmed VITT cases and 81 deaths in the UK alone. The company maintained the vaccine had saved over 6.5 million lives in its first year.

Baroness Hallett's COVID-19 Inquiry Module 4 report, published in April 2026, called the scheme "not sufficiently supportive" and demanded urgent reform: raise the £120,000 payment at least in line with inflation (suggesting over £200,000), introduce graduated payments by degree of injury, and scrap or soften the 60% threshold that leaves people with significant neurological damage with nothing.

The government published its response on 16 October 2026, accepting the need for reform and committing to a review to make the scheme "fit for purpose and delivered effectively," while noting concerns over administrative costs.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesman offered "deepest sympathies" and said officials were carefully considering the recommendations.

More than 24,260 COVID-related claims had reached the scheme by 30 June 2026, yet only 264 resulted in awards - just over 1%. Roughly 580-603 claims had causation accepted by medical assessors yet failed the 60% disability bar.

Running costs since April 2022 hit £83 million, more than double the roughly £32 million paid to victims. Transverse myelitis was later listed among the vaccine's extremely rare side effects, and dosing intervals were widened after cases like Hoyle's.

Officials maintained benefits outweighed risks, but the scheme's design - built for older industrial-style injuries - fits poorly with the neurological, fluctuating, and sometimes partially recovering harms seen with these products.

Patterns of injury have been gradually acknowledged. Last year, Post-Vaccination Syndrome research from Yale was published, documenting high rates of brain fog, exercise intolerance, extreme fatigue, sleep disruption, tingling or numbness, and confirmed signals for myocarditis, tinnitus, thrombosis with thrombocytopenia, and Guillain-Barré Syndrome.

A Taiwanese study of 467 healthcare workers, all of whom had received at least three doses, found neurological and psychiatric symptoms matching "long COVID" in a group that had never been infected.

Of the 222 with no record of infection and negative nucleoprotein antibodies, more than 30% reported mild fatigue, nearly 10% reported trouble concentrating, and 11.7% reported worsening memory.

The authors noted no statistically significant difference in symptom severity between those with confirmed infection, asymptomatic infection, and those never infected, yet did not examine vaccination as a possible cause.

A South Korean cohort study of more than 8.4 million people, published in Biomarker Research in September 2025, reported associations between COVID-19 vaccination and elevated risks of six cancers.

Booster doses were linked to a 125% increase in pancreatic cancer risk. Prostate cancer risk rose 69%, lung cancer 53%, thyroid 35%, gastric 34%, colorectal 28%, and breast 20%.

The authors stated that "COVID-19 vaccination could be associated with an increased risk of six specific cancer types" and noted that booster doses substantially affected risks for gastric and pancreatic cancers.

In the United States, the picture is similarly lopsided. The Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program (CICP), which covers COVID vaccines, had received 14,250 claims by 1 October 2026, the bulk alleging vaccine injury. Of 8,369 decisions, only 66 had been compensated and 120 found eligible.

A Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations hearing in April 2026 examined VAERS data showing COVID vaccines associated with more adverse events and deaths than all other vaccines combined over the system's history, including rates 55 times higher for deaths than the flu vaccine. FDA staff had flagged masking of safety signals and were ordered to stop certain analyses.

Myocarditis and pericarditis signals for the mRNA vaccines appeared in Israel within a month of rollout in early 2021. Israel shared the data with the CDC and EMA in February, yet public and clinician alerts came only months later, after most eligible young people had already received two doses.

An Oxford analysis found an eight-fold risk of myocarditis in under-40s within a week of a second Pfizer dose and a 44-fold risk after Moderna. Hong Kong reported a one-in-3,000 risk in adolescent boys after a second dose and switched to a single-dose policy.

A Thai study of teenagers found 29% with signs of heart disturbance after a second Pfizer dose. No comparable reckoning has followed the delayed disclosure.

In Australia, FOI documents showed 35 people died on the same day as their COVID vaccination. The Therapeutic Goods Administration completed causality assessments for only 24 of them and referred none to its Vaccine Safety Investigation Group.

Of more than 1,000 deaths reported to the TGA's database, only 14 were officially linked to the vaccines. Where timing data existed, one in four occurred within three days and 39% within a week.

Dr Suzanne Niblett called the claim of thorough review "very misleading" when most cases had not been properly analysed. Dr Rado Faleti noted that in the vaccine-injured community, "not a single person reports being followed-up or investigated by the TGA."

Meanwhile, new Moderna formulations for the 2026-2027 season received FDA approval in late August 2026, 81 days before the scheduled start of the human Phase 3b/4 safety and immunogenicity study.

Legislation introduced in September 2026 would further tilt the process: S. 3323 would require the CDC director to adopt ACIP recommendations unless unsupported by a preponderance of peer-reviewed evidence, while raising the bar for withdrawing recommendations or removing entries from the Vaccine Injury Table.

Hoyle's case is not isolated. Hundreds of people whose injuries medical assessors linked to the vaccines sit below the arbitrary 60% line and receive nothing from the state scheme, even as the bureaucracy costs more than the payouts.

The inquiry has forced an official admission that the current rules do not match the injuries that occurred. Whether the promised review produces real graduated support or simply more process remains to be seen.

People who stepped forward under official assurances of safety and necessity now face the same bureaucratic gatekeeping that defined the rollout.

Accountability for the injuries, and the freedom to weigh risks without coercion or denial, still lag behind the volume of claims.

title: US Army Commander Thought This New Technology Was "Crazy" - Until He Saw It In Action
desc:
US Army Commander Thought This New Technology Was "Crazy" - Until He Saw It In Action

A top U.S. Army commander has revealed how a once-dismissed military technology is emerging as a potentially game-changing weapon of modern warfare, capable of spying on enemy territory, launching drones and supporting military operations from the edge of space.

Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army's Space and Missile Defense Command, admitted he initially thought the idea of deploying high-altitude balloons for military missions sounded absurd.

The technology has already been deployed to support U.S. military operations in the Middle East, according to The War Zone.

"It just sounded crazy to me that we were considering this," Rafferty acknowledged during a media roundtable at the Association of the U.S. Army's annual convention.

Lt. Gen. Rafferty's skepticism evaporated after witnessing the balloons during military exercises in Morocco.

"I saw the high-altitude balloons in action, and I was immediately convinced," he said said, describing their capabilities as "game-changing."

Unlike conventional aircraft, the balloons can remain airborne for days, weeks or potentially months, operating at altitudes exceeding 60,000 feet while carrying sophisticated surveillance equipment.

The systems could also serve as communications hubs and launch platforms for drone swarms, potentially extending the military's reach deep into contested territory.

Army Col. Joseph Mroszczyk said the service is exploring a family of balloon systems operating between 60,000 and 100,000 feet, effectively bridging the gap between traditional aircraft and satellites.

"In my former role as an MDTF commander, we experimented a lot in the Pacific with those [balloon-based] capabilities. We have leveraged different size platforms," Col. Mroszczyk told TWZ. "In this [TID-Space Superiority] role, as a proponent, what I'm pushing for is a family of stratospheric systems that really covers smaller size all the way up to larger size types of platforms in terms of balloons."

"What that enables us to provide is space-like capabilities, really exploiting a transition point between what is normally considered the aerial layer and the space domain," he added.
