title: The Precious Metals Crisis That Could Trigger A Global Financial Reckoning
desc:
The Precious Metals Crisis That Could Trigger A Global Financial Reckoning

Authored by Milan Adams via Preppgroup,

It ended, apparently, in the spring. Gold ran to a record in the last days of January 2026 - $5,608 an ounce on one spot reading, roughly $5,405 on the LBMA benchmark, and $5,318.40 on COMEX futures, three figures describing the same metal and differing by nearly $300, which is a reminder that the price depends on which price you mean - and then it simply stopped. By the middle of October the metal was changing hands near $4,112, some 27 per cent below the January spot peak, while silver, having briefly touched $121.62 on 29 January, had lost more than half its value and was trading around $56. Two metals, two collapses, and for anyone who had spent three years waiting for the precious metals complex to deflate and stop interrupting the serious business of equity markets, a comfortable conclusion was available: the thing had been a trade, the trade had unwound, and the world could return to its previous arrangements.

The underlying market, though, had already changed, and the sell-off made the shift harder to ignore.

Between April and June of 2026, as the price fell and commentary turned sceptical, central banks bought 288.9 tonnes of gold, the highest second-quarter total on record and 62 per cent above the same period a year earlier. The quarterly figure does not by itself prove that the buying was concentrated in the weakest weeks, but the World Gold Council's own reporting indicates that institutions kept adding through a quarter in which gold lost 14 per cent, which is the opposite of the pattern one would expect from buyers chasing a rally. And they did so in size and without much explanation.

Silver spent the same year doing something the price chart could not show. The market recorded a sixth consecutive annual supply deficit, estimated by the Silver Institute's World Silver Survey 2026 at 46.3 million ounces against 40.3 million the year before, with mine production flat. Despite the 53 per cent decline in the price, the projected shortfall widened.

That pairing - a violent correction alongside a deteriorating physical balance - is the substance of what follows. The word shock has been devalued by overuse, and precision is worth the trouble here. A shock, as the term is used in this article, is not a spike on a screen or the sort of one-week convulsion that produces memorable charts and forgettable analysis. It is closer to a condition: the moment when the price of a metal and the physical availability of that metal stop agreeing with one another, and the gap becomes large enough that ordinary arbitrage can no longer close it. Price spikes are events. What gold and silver have been signalling is a change in the settlement mechanics of the world economy, and events of that kind are considerably harder to reverse than the enthusiasm or the panic surrounding them.

Part of the reason this has gone relatively unexamined is that precious metals sit at an awkward angle to the way financial news is organised. They are not a technology, so they generate no product launches. They are not an earnings story, so they produce no quarterly surprises of the kind that fill column inches. Their most consequential movements are recorded in the technical backwater of lease rates, exchange-for-physical spreads and official reserve statistics, and their significance only becomes legible when several of those readings are placed side by side. Meanwhile the attention of the investing public has been directed elsewhere with considerable efficiency - toward artificial intelligence, toward a handful of large-cap equities, toward the political calendar - while the foundations of the monetary order have been quietly rearranged by the very institutions whose job it is to maintain them.

Gold is behaving the way an asset behaves when sovereign institutions begin treating it as a reserve again rather than as a diversification, and silver is behaving the way a metal behaves when its industrial consumption outruns its ability to be produced. These are two different mechanisms producing two different prices, but they are pointing in the same direction, and the direction concerns confidence: confidence in the financial system in the first case, confidence in the productive system in the second. When both begin to erode at once, the practical consequences run through supply chains, borrowing costs, defence procurement and ultimately consumer prices, and they do so with a lag long enough to be politically comfortable and short enough to be economically unpleasant.

A word on method before the evidence. Some of what follows is documented and can be stated flatly, with the source attached. Some is inference drawn from the data by the author, and will be marked as such. A smaller part is speculation, and the reader is entitled to know which claims sit in which category. The central bank figures, in particular, deserve the scepticism set out later in this piece: they are estimates, they are revised, and one of them was revised in 2026 by nearly four-fifths. Anyone who tells you with confidence what the official sector did last quarter is working from numbers that may not survive the next data release, and the direction of travel is more reliable than any single measurement of it.

The current configuration differs from the rallies of 1980 and 2011 in one respect that matters more than the scale of any price move, and that is the composition of the bid behind it. The 1980 episode was a genuine monetary crisis - double-digit inflation, an oil shock, a dollar in retreat - and it coincided with a leveraged attempt by two brothers, Nelson Bunker and William Herbert Hunt, to corner the silver market. Gold peaked near $850 an ounce on 21 January 1980; silver touched roughly $50 before collapsing in late March, when the Hunts could not meet a margin call, an episode still remembered as Silver Thursday. The Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker had already driven the federal funds rate toward 20 per cent that spring, and would do so again in 1981. The two metals moved on related but distinct clocks, and silver's collapse owed at least as much to leverage as to monetary policy. The 2011 spike was a policy trade: quantitative easing, a European sovereign-debt crisis, a Treasury downgrade, unwound when the policy trade unwound. Both were financial events with financial causes. What distinguishes the present moment is that it is underwritten by balance sheets with no intention of selling and pressed upward by physical consumption that cannot easily be switched off, and that is a harder thing to deflate than a position.

Which brings the discussion to a sentence spoken in 1912 that has been quoted so often it has lost some of its bite, and deserves to have it restored. John Pierpont Morgan, testifying before the Pujo Committee of the United States House of Representatives, was asked to define money.

"Money is gold, and nothing else." - J. P. Morgan, testimony before the Pujo Committee, 1912.

What fell, and what did not

To understand why the spring drawdown changed so little, it helps to know what actually happened in the London market during the winter, because the dislocation there was more revealing than the headline prices suggest.

The pressure began building in the final weeks of 2025 and broke in January. Silver rose 25 per cent in a fortnight at one point, and the gold-to-silver ratio - the number of ounces of silver needed to buy a single ounce of gold - fell below 45, a level rarely visited outside periods of outright stress. Silver's all-time high of $121.62, struck on 29 January, arrived not through gradual repricing but through a squeeze, with the characteristic signature of one: lease rates for physical silver spiking as borrowers scrambled to cover short positions, forward curves inverting, and a widening exchange-for-physical spread between the London over-the-counter market and the New York futures exchange that told anyone reading it the two venues had temporarily stopped pricing the same commodity.

When a squeeze of that kind unwinds, the price usually collapses, and this one obliged. Silver lost more than half its value between late January and the autumn. Gold, the more liquid and more heavily institutionally held of the two, lost rather less - roughly 27 per cent - and the ratio drifted back out toward 70, close to its long-run average.

The squeeze cleared, as squeezes do, because the high price performed three functions at once: it destroyed marginal demand, it liberated hoarded metal from private hands, and it attracted new short sellers. In 2026 the first two functions operated weakly. Industrial consumers kept buying, because a solar manufacturer or a connector maker does not shut a production line because the input costs 30 per cent more than last quarter; it absorbs the cost and passes what it can downstream. Private holders in Asia, whose accumulation behaviour is discussed below, largely held. What did the work of unwinding the squeeze was the third function: financial sellers, in the form of futures and options positioning, pressing the paper price down until the physical premium vanished. The unwinding happened in the paper market. The metal itself did not become any more abundant, and two months later the deficit projection for the year was revised wider.

Official understanding of all this has always been shaky, and the most senior economist in the world once admitted as much. Ben Bernanke, delivering a lecture at George Washington University in 2013, was asked about the metal and gave an answer of unusual candour.

"Nobody understands gold prices, and I don't pretend to either." - Ben Bernanke, George Washington University, 2013.

Bernanke's broader position, offered in Senate testimony two years earlier, was the more consequential one for policy: "Gold isn't money, it's an asset," he told the Banking Committee in 2011. The two statements sit awkwardly beside each other - an asset whose price nobody understands, and whose monetary role has supposedly been retired - and that awkwardness is a fair description of where the official sector has been for a generation. It is also why the behaviour of reserve managers in 2026 carries more weight than any speech: they are acting on a view of gold that contradicts the doctrine their predecessors wrote down.

The bid that does not trade

Reserve accumulation by central banks is not a new habit; it is an old one interrupted by the anomalous quarter-century between the end of Bretton Woods and the financial crisis of 2008. Novelty lies elsewhere - in who is buying, in what they say about why, and in their demonstrated indifference to price. All three have changed since 2022, and the change is documented by the institutions themselves.

The World Gold Council's ninth Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey, published in 2026, reported that 89 per cent of central bankers expected global gold reserves to rise over the following twelve months, while a record 45 per cent expected their own institution's holdings to grow. An HSBC survey of reserve managers the same year put the share planning additions near 40 per cent, with a majority of those respondents stating explicitly that current prices would not deter them. Reserve managers are, by temperament, the most price-sensitive cohort in finance; they buy weakness and rotate out of strength. In 2026 they inverted the habit knowingly.

Morgan Stanley research circulated during the year found that gold had come to represent a larger share of global central bank reserves than United States Treasuries - the first such reading since 1996. The instrument that anchored the post-war monetary order, and that every emerging-market central bank was once instructed to accumulate as a matter of prudence, has been demoted inside the official sector's own portfolio. Not abandoned; demoted. The distinction matters, because it points to diversification rather than panic.

Who is doing the buying matters as much as the total. The post-2022 acceleration was led by institutions with concrete reasons to want distance from the dollar clearing system, and the immobilisation of Russia's reserves supplied the template for every reserve manager with a sanctions exposure. China's disclosed holdings have risen steadily, but the more interesting Chinese figure is the one absent from the statistics - the widely held inference, supported by trade-flow analysis rather than by published numbers, that true holdings exceed reported ones by a margin large enough to matter. Poland, Türkiye, India, Singapore and a rotating group of Gulf and Central Asian institutions have all added. Nothing about the pattern is ideological. It is defensive, and it is being executed by states that have watched the rules of the reserve system be rewritten by its largest participant.

One consequence of this goes largely unremarked and will matter if the trajectory holds. Reserve gold is not traded. It moves between vaults and then sits, sometimes for decades, so each tonne purchased and placed in an official vault is withdrawn from the float available to settle transactions in the market that actually sets the price. Estimates of London's free float - the metal genuinely available for settlement - cluster between 3,000 and 4,000 tonnes, though the figure is inferred rather than published and the London Bullion Market Association's reporting does not permit a precise calculation. Against a float of that size, 289 tonnes in ninety days is not a rounding error. It is somewhere near 8 per cent of the tradable stock absorbed in a single quarter, by buyers who will not sell it back. The arithmetic should be treated as an order of magnitude rather than a measurement, since not every tonne an official institution buys necessarily comes out of that float, and some purchases are settled from metal that was already sitting in a vault rather than from stock that would otherwise have traded.

An honest treatment of this material has to include the counterexample, and 2026 supplied a large one. The World Gold Council's initial estimate of first-quarter central bank demand was 244 tonnes, widely reported as evidence of sovereign conviction at scale. In its second-quarter release the Council revised that figure to 57 tonnes, following new data and analysis - a swing of nearly 190 tonnes, or roughly four-fifths of the original number. The revision was absorbed into the next data release without the fanfare that had greeted the first figure.

Two conclusions follow. Central bank demand is genuinely difficult to measure, because reporting is uneven, because some purchases are routed through sovereign wealth funds and state oil funds whose holdings are counted inconsistently, and because the boundary between reserve gold and state-owned commercial gold is not always clean. And the direction of travel survives revision in a way that no individual data point does. A four-year pattern documented across multiple sources is not overturned by a restatement of one quarter, and it is not explained by the surveys continuing to record near-unanimous intention to keep buying. If the accumulation were an artefact, the people doing it would have stopped saying they intended to continue.

Gold's floor, then, is the standing policy of several dozen sovereign institutions rather than a technical price level, and the cost of that support is worth naming: as the official bid absorbs more of the float, upside becomes less a matter of speculative enthusiasm and more a matter of arithmetic - how many tonnes remain available to buy.

No one has framed the underlying logic more brutally than Alan Greenspan, writing in 1966 as a young economist, decades before he acquired the reputation that defined his later career. His essay Gold and Economic Freedom contains a sentence that reads, in 2026, less like libertarian theory than like a description of the world.

"In the absence of the gold standard, there is no way to protect savings from confiscation through inflation." - Alan Greenspan, "Gold and Economic Freedom," 1966.

The sixth year, and the metal that does not come back

Silver's position is the more instructive of the two, precisely because it attracts less commentary. Gold is a monetary object and monetary objects invite narrative. Silver is consumed, which makes it duller to write about and considerably more revealing.

The Silver Institute's World Silver Survey 2026, produced by the consultancy Metals Focus, projected a global shortfall of 46.3 million ounces for the year against 40.3 million in 2025 - a sixth consecutive annual deficit, with mine production flat. Secondary coverage of the same report has circulated a competing figure of 215 million ounces for the year; the two numbers do not reconcile cleanly and the Institute's own headline is the smaller one, but the direction is not in dispute in either version. Cumulative deficits since 2021 have drawn above-ground inventories down to a cushion thinner than at any point in the modern era. That the deficits are real is a matter of record. That they must eventually produce a shortage, and higher prices, is an inference, and a reasonable one, but it rests on the assumption that demand keeps growing and supply keeps failing to respond.

The difference between the two metals is mechanical. Gold, once mined, is nearly all still with us - in bars, coins, jewellery, official vaults and exchange-traded funds - and very little is ever destroyed, which means the gold market's deficits are reallocations between holders rather than shortages in any absolute sense; the metal can always be found at a price. Silver does not work that way. Somewhere between half and 60 per cent of annual consumption enters industrial applications where the metal is dispersed into finished goods in quantities too small to recover economically. A solar panel holds perhaps fifteen to twenty grammes. A high-speed connector holds a fraction of one. A pacemaker, a photovoltaic ribbon, an automotive sensor, a server board - each carries a trace, and when the product is scrapped the trace usually goes with it.

The result is a one-way flow that separates silver from every other precious metal. Roughly half of each year's mine supply leaves the monetary system permanently, entering the industrial one, where it becomes subject to substitution pressure, thrifting and eventual landfill. What remains circulates, but against a base that is being eaten. Year after year of deficits do not merely tighten a market; they convert a monetary asset into an industrial one, tonne by tonne, until the residual monetary stock is small enough to be squeezed - which is precisely what happened in January, when the price briefly cleared $121 and the ratio collapsed below 45.

A further asymmetry eludes the balance sheets. Because so much silver ends up in finished products, the metal's price elasticity of supply is close to zero over any relevant horizon. A high price does not bring forward metal the way it does in a market with spare capacity; what it brings is a decision to build, and the building takes years. In the interim, high prices encourage thrifting in the very industries that need the metal, which reduces demand slightly, which relieves the deficit slightly, which encourages complacency, which delays the investment that would actually solve the problem. The cycle is self-defeating, and it has been running for six years.

Keith Neumeyer, chief executive of First Majestic Silver, has spent much of the past decade making a version of this argument in public, and has repeatedly said in interviews that the metal should trade between $100 and $200 an ounce. In 2026, having touched $121 and retreated, he looked less eccentric than he had in 2016.

"The market is going to wake up one day and there won't be any silver." - Keith Neumeyer, chief executive of First Majestic Silver, in repeated interviews with Kitco News.

A deficit that widened while demand fell

The strangest part of the silver story is also the least reported.

Silver's largest single industrial end-market is photovoltaics. Solar manufacturing absorbed 186.6 million ounces in 2025, having grown from roughly 11 per cent of industrial demand in 2014 to nearly 29 per cent a decade later - a near-tripling of share driven by the sheer volume of panels installed worldwide. Then something happened that the bullish case had not fully anticipated: the industry began to thrift. Manufacturers, squeezed by collapsing panel prices and under pressure to cut bill-of-materials costs, reduced the silver loading per cell through thinner fingers, improved pastes and a shift toward alternative metallisation. Photovoltaic demand fell 6 per cent in 2025 and was forecast to fall a further 19 per cent in 2026, to roughly 151 million ounces - the largest annual decline on record for silver's biggest industrial customer.

On a naive reading, a 19 per cent collapse in the largest demand segment should have cured the deficit. It did the opposite. The 2026 shortfall is projected wider than 2025's.

What grows while solar retreats explains the rest. Total industrial offtake slipped 3 per cent in 2025 to 657.4 million ounces, the first post-pandemic decline, and was forecast to fall a further 3 per cent in 2026 to roughly 639.6 million. Beneath that aggregate, the composition is shifting. Demand linked to data-centre construction, high-speed transmission hardware, electric-vehicle penetration, charging infrastructure and grid modernisation is expanding, and it is expanding in applications where silver resists substitution. A photovoltaic manufacturer can redesign a cell to use less silver. A high-voltage connector, a switchgear contact, a silver-sintered power module in a server rack - these have far less room to manoeuvre, because the metal's conductivity is not decorative. It is functional.

So the market absorbed the loss of 35 million ounces of solar demand and still ran a wider deficit, because what replaced solar was less thriftable and more numerous. This is the detail that separates the present cycle from a normal commodity correction. Demand destruction in the largest segment produced a deficit, not a surplus, and it did so in the same year that mine supply stayed flat and official-sector gold purchases set a record.

Eleven years between a price and a mine

The most common objection to the supply-deficit argument is that higher prices will eventually summon more metal. That is true, and largely irrelevant over any horizon a policymaker or an investor cares about, because the lag between a price signal and a tonne of refined silver is measured in years and occasionally in decades.

Discovering an economically viable deposit has become harder. Average ore grades have declined across the major producing regions for a generation, which means more rock must be moved, crushed and processed to yield the same quantity of metal - a direct increase in energy and capital intensity at precisely the moment both have become more expensive. Environmental permitting has lengthened in most jurisdictions, and in several important ones it now routinely exceeds a decade from discovery to first production. Financing costs remain far above the levels of the 2010s, which raises the hurdle rate for any project and eliminates the marginal ones. And the industry's own capital discipline, imposed by shareholders after two decades of value destruction, means that even producers with cash are reluctant to build.

Set against this, the demand side requires almost no new investment at all. A data centre is financed and built within eighteen months. A solar farm is commissioned in a year. An electric-vehicle plant is retooled in two. The industrial base can therefore expand its consumption of silver on a cycle roughly one-fifth the length of the cycle required to expand supply, and it has been doing so since 2021.

Some numbers, arranged as they would appear on a desk blotter, make the asymmetry easier to hold in the head. Each is sourced, and the risk markers are the author's own reading of the data rather than an official classification: they reflect how far each line has moved from its own long-run average, and how much of the adjustment would have to come from price rather than from supply or demand responding.

The float, the vault, and the lease rate

Anyone wanting to test whether the physical market is genuinely tight should ignore the spot price and look instead at three instruments almost nobody reports: the lease rate, the forward curve, and the exchange-for-physical spread between London and New York.

Lease rates measure the cost of borrowing metal. In a comfortable market they hover near the risk-free rate and attract no attention. When they spike, it means holders of short positions cannot find physical metal to deliver and are paying up to borrow it - a condition that, in extremis, forces the kind of squeeze that drove silver through $121 in January. The forward curve tells the same story in a different register: a market in contango, where later delivery is more expensive than immediate delivery, is comfortable, while backwardation, where immediate metal commands a premium over future delivery, is the signature of scarcity. Backwardation appeared in silver during the winter dislocation and reappeared intermittently through the spring.

The exchange-for-physical spread is the more arcane of the three, and the most diagnostic. It measures the gap between the London over-the-counter price and the New York futures price. When that gap widens beyond the cost of shipping and insuring metal across the Atlantic, it tells you that one venue has run short of deliverable material and the other has not - that the two are no longer pricing the same commodity. This happened in silver in early 2021, when the spread blew out in a manner that briefly threatened the futures exchange's delivery mechanism, and again in the winter of 2025-26. The precedent matters because the 2021 episode was resolved not by new supply but by a large redirection of existing metal from London to New York, which drew down London's float and left the system more fragile than before. Each resolution of a squeeze has made the next one easier, though that is a tendency rather than a law.

These readings matter more than the spot price because the spot price can be moved by paper. A sufficiently determined financial seller can press the futures price down without owning any metal, and in 2026 that is largely what happened. London's float was not rebuilt, and the deficit did not close. What the drawdown removed was speculative positioning, not supply.

The current environment, then, is not a bubble unwinding. A bubble unwinds when the asset returns to its natural owners, and in gold and silver the natural owners - central banks and industrial consumers respectively - have been the marginal buyers throughout. No obvious cohort of holders appears to be waiting to sell into a rally, though that is an observation about what is visible rather than a proof that none exists. It is at least consistent with the record prices of January failing to produce a wave of profit-taking at scale.

Tariffs pointed at metal

Trade policy has applied a second pressure, less discussed than geology and more immediately consequential.

In November 2025, silver and the platinum-group metals were added to the United States Geological Survey's list of critical minerals. The designation triggered an investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, the statute that permits the president to restrict imports on national-security grounds. Under that process the administration had ninety days to decide whether to act, and the market spent the interval pricing the possibility of tariffs on refined silver entering the United States - a prospect with an obvious consequence, since a tariff on silver would pull metal toward America and away from London, exactly the mechanism that had drained the London float in 2021.

On 14 January 2026 the president issued a proclamation declining, for the time being, to impose tariffs on processed critical minerals and their derivative products, while directing the relevant agencies toward trade negotiations with partner countries. Two further proclamations were published in the Federal Register on 20 January. The details are dense and the tariff schedules obscure, but the strategic posture is not: a duty was imposed on certain categories while precious metals were, for now, left outside. Silver had been excluded from the reciprocal tariff schedules the previous September, alongside other critical minerals then under investigation.

In effect, the world's largest economy has built a mechanism capable of redirecting the global flow of silver at short notice, and has not yet pulled the trigger. The metal currently moves freely; the threat of restriction does the work. Any decision to activate the tariff would pull physical silver into American warehouses, tighten London further, and widen the exchange-for-physical spread - the same sequence that preceded the 2021 dislocation, but into a market with a smaller float and a sixth consecutive deficit behind it.

A comparable logic operates in the other direction. China has spent the past several years converting its dominance in processing into leverage over the countries that consume what it processes, and the instruments of that leverage - export licences, quota systems, state-controlled allocation - are applied to critical materials with increasing frequency. The precise restrictions change from quarter to quarter and the reporting is imperfect, which is itself a source of cost, because a manufacturer cannot plan a five-year plant around a policy it cannot read.

The precedent is uncomfortable. Richard Nixon, announcing the suspension of dollar convertibility into gold on 15 August 1971, framed the decision as an act of monetary stewardship, and in a narrow sense it was. What he did not say, because it was not yet clear, was that severing the last formal link between a major currency and a physical metal would set in motion a half-century of competition between financial assets and tangible ones, with the state structurally on the side of the former.

The bill arriving

Behind all of this sits the arithmetic that no amount of commodity analysis can alter, because it is a matter of law and demography rather than of geology or sentiment.

The United States ran a federal deficit of roughly $2 trillion in fiscal 2026, on the estimate of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, which put interest expense at about $1.1 trillion - a record 3.4 per cent of gross domestic product and the second-largest line item in the budget, ahead of defence and ahead of Medicare. The Congressional Budget Office, working on its own conventions for net interest, projects a figure nearer $1 trillion for the year and a rise from 3.3 per cent of GDP to 4.6 per cent by 2036, on the assumption that nothing dramatic changes. Penn Wharton's budget model has produced estimates suggesting that stabilising the debt ratio would require permanent fiscal adjustment of a few percentage points of GDP, sustained over decades.

The link to precious metals is not the crude claim that deficits cause gold to rise; over short horizons the relationship is unstable and the correlation unreliable. A narrower claim survives scrutiny. A government facing rising interest costs and slowing growth has fewer politically available options. Raising taxes risks suppressing investment. Cutting spending risks recession. Borrowing more only defers the pressure. What remains, in the end, is the quiet erosion of the currency's purchasing power - the mechanism Greenspan described in 1966 - and the more the erosion is engineered, the more attractive an asset with no counterparty becomes.

Ray Dalio put the shorter version of this to an audience at Davos in January 2020, at a moment when the formulation seemed merely provocative.

"Cash is trash." - Ray Dalio, World Economic Forum, Davos, January 2020.

Dalio's fuller argument, made over several years, is that the debt cycle had matured to the point where the world's major central banks would be forced to monetise liabilities rather than let yields rise, and that holders of currency would bear the cost. Six years later, with interest consuming 3.4 per cent of American output and rising, the argument looks less like a provocation and more like a partial forecast that has begun to come true.

Three economies, three traps

Generalisations about "the global economy" conceal three quite different situations, and the differences matter for how each is likely to respond.

China's growth engine has been tied to strategic commodities for three decades, and its current position is the most delicate of the three. Property-sector weakness, cautious household spending and slowing export momentum have narrowed the policy space, while the state's habit of accumulating physical assets during uncertainty has been reproduced at the household level with unusual fidelity. Chinese retail demand for gold has repeatedly surged whenever domestic financial confidence has dipped, and the metal functions there less as an investment than as an insurance policy held outside the banking system - a behaviour with deep historical roots and no obvious substitute. Meanwhile Beijing's own reserve accumulation, partly disclosed and partly inferred, has continued.

The American position is different in kind. Deep capital markets, technological leadership and the dollar's reserve status continue to supply resilience, and resilience should not be confused with immunity. Persistent deficits, rising interest costs, political polarisation and an active trade agenda have combined to make fiscal decisions progressively more expensive, while manufacturers attempting to rebuild domestic supply chains encounter higher labour costs, dearer imported components and uncertain access to strategic materials. The reshoring project, in other words, is being executed at precisely the moment the inputs it requires have become most expensive.

Europe's trap is the most self-inflicted. The continent has committed to an energy transition and an industrial strategy that depend heavily on reliable access to critical materials, while possessing limited domestic mining and a permitting regime that makes new extraction slow even by global standards. The result is a bloc structurally short of exactly the commodities its own policy has made most valuable, with the added complication that its manufacturing base competes against Asian producers with more direct access to supply.

Zoltan Pozsar, then at Credit Suisse, published a note in March 2022 whose central claim has aged unusually well. He argued that the freezing of Russia's reserves had fractured the assumptions underpinning the dollar-based financial order, and that what followed would be organised around commodities rather than around credit.

"We are about to witness the birth of Bretton Woods III." - Zoltan Pozsar, Credit Suisse, March 2022.

Whether the label is accurate is debatable; the substance - that reserves would be held in things rather than in promises - has been borne out by four years of official-sector behaviour.

The machines that eat silver

If the deficits are structural, the reason is that the demand driving them is not discretionary. Silver is not bought by these industries because it is fashionable or because a manager likes the chart. It is bought because the alternatives perform worse, and in several applications there is no alternative at all.

The list is longer than most people assume, and it grows with each round of capital expenditure in the sectors governments have designated strategic:

  • Data centres and their power trains, where silver-bearing contacts, sintered modules and high-speed interconnects are consumed at a density that scales with computational load rather than with floor area - meaning the build-out of artificial-intelligence infrastructure raises silver intensity per square metre even as the buildings themselves become more efficient.
  • Electrical grids, the least glamorous and most consequential of the categories, since every connection, breaker, contactor and transformer involves silver in small quantities multiplied by an enormous installed base; grid renewal programmes in Europe, China and the United States are all now underway simultaneously.
  • Photovoltaics, retreating in intensity per cell but still the single largest consumer, and expanding in installed volume at a rate that has so far offset the thrifting.
  • Electric vehicles and charging infrastructure, where silver content per vehicle is materially higher than in a combustion car, concentrated in power electronics and high-voltage connections.
  • Defence procurement, a category that has expanded sharply and that operates almost entirely outside price sensitivity, since a government buying a guided system does not renegotiate because a metal moved.
  • Medical devices, including implantables and diagnostic equipment, where the quantities are trivial and the requirement absolute.

All of these are downstream of decisions already taken. A grid renewal programme authorised in 2024 consumes silver in 2027. An electric-vehicle platform designed in 2023 locks in its material bill of materials for a decade. Solar capacity installed this year will still be generating in 2050. The demand, in other words, is largely pre-committed, and it was committed before anyone thought carefully about whether the supply existed.

Why price stopped working as a signal

Shortages are supposed to cure themselves through price. Something like that has been happening in silver, and it has not been sufficient, because the elasticity of demand in its principal uses is low and the elasticity of supply is close to zero, so the burden of adjustment falls on price almost entirely, which means price must move a great deal to achieve a modest rebalancing.

Consider a solar manufacturer facing a 40 per cent rise in its silver cost. The metal is perhaps 10 to 15 per cent of the module's bill of materials, so the direct impact is a few percentage points. The obvious response is to redesign toward thinner fingers and better pastes - which the industry has done, reducing intensity by a fifth in a single year. But that response has a floor, because at some point the fingers become too thin to print reliably and the paste chemistry runs out of room. Having reached that floor, the manufacturer's demand becomes almost completely price-insensitive: it will pay whatever the metal costs, because the alternative is not producing.

On the supply side the situation is worse. The decision to build a mine is made on a price forecast that must hold for a decade, and a price that spikes for eighteen months and then halves - precisely what happened in 2026 - is the least helpful possible signal. It encourages over-investment at the top and then punishes it, which is one reason the industry has been so reluctant to commit despite the best margins in a generation. Mining executives have learned, at considerable cost, that a high price today is weak evidence of a high price in 2034.

Warren Buffett supplied the essential scepticism about the whole enterprise in his 2011 letter to shareholders, and it is worth holding alongside the bullish case rather than against it.

"Gold gets dug out of the ground... then we melt it down, dig another hole, bury it again and pay people to stand around guarding it." - Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter, 2011.

Buffett's point was that an asset with no cash flow is only worth what the next buyer will pay. What has changed since 2011 is that a significant share of the next buyers are now sovereign institutions whose motives are political rather than financial, and who are therefore indifferent to the absence of cash flow. For them, the absence of a counterparty is the point.

What the forecasters disagree about

Forecasts are usually read for their numbers and should be read for their dispersion, and 2026 supplied an unusually wide one.

Goldman Sachs research published during the year put gold at $4,900 an ounce by the end of 2026. J.P. Morgan's commodity team went considerably further, projecting an average of $6,000 in the final quarter and $6,300 by the end of 2027, before a round of downward revisions pulled the consensus toward $4,500 by year-end. On silver, J.P. Morgan forecast $63 in the fourth quarter - a level the metal had already exceeded before retreating. BullionVault's aggregate of several forecasting models put silver above $80 by December.

The forecasts differ, as they always do, but the disagreement here is structural rather than marginal. The bears are working from a monetary framework in which higher-for-longer rates suppress non-yielding assets, and on that framework gold above $4,000 is expensive. The bulls are working from a reserve-and-physical framework in which the identity of the marginal buyer has changed, and on that framework the price is a residual of quantity demanded against a shrinking float. The two models do not share assumptions, so additional data alone will not reconcile them, though it may force one side to revise the assumptions themselves. One framework will be vindicated by events, and the vindication will tell you which was correct - but only afterwards.

A reasonable position, and the one this piece adopts, is that the bearish case is stronger on a twelve-month view and the bullish case is stronger on a five-year view, and that the two are compatible. A monetary tightening that suppresses gold in 2027 does not close a silver deficit or persuade a central bank to sell. Time horizons are doing most of the work in this argument, and much of the public disagreement about precious metals is really a disagreement about duration dressed up as a disagreement about facts.

Three ways this ends

It is worth setting out the possibilities plainly, without assigning false precision to the probabilities.

  • Managed re-rating. Gold and silver grind higher over several years, punctuated by drawdowns like the one in 2026. Mining investment eventually responds, new supply arrives in the early 2030s, the deficit narrows, and the metals settle at a permanently higher plateau without any crisis. This is the least dramatic outcome and, on the evidence, the most probable. It requires nothing more than continued official-sector accumulation and continued industrial demand, both of which are already in place.
  • Disorderly squeeze. A tariff decision, a policy error, or an unanticipated inventory draw triggers another episode like January's, but into a market with a smaller float and thinner dealer balance sheets. The price overshoots violently, industrial consumers are forced to buy at any level to keep lines running, and the dislocation propagates into manufacturer margins, then into component prices, then into consumer electronics and construction costs. This scenario requires no new development, only the repetition of something that has already happened once this year.
  • Rupture. A broader monetary or fiscal event - a failed auction, a currency crisis in a large emerging economy, a disorderly repricing of sovereign debt - forces a step-change in how reserves are held. Gold rises severalfold rather than advancing by a modest percentage, the official sector's accumulation accelerates into something closer to a scramble, and the existing architecture of the reserve system is formally, rather than informally, abandoned. This is the least likely and the most consequential, and it is the scenario in which the phrase precious metals shock earns its name.

What would have to be true

Intellectual honesty requires stating the conditions under which the argument above would be wrong, because a thesis that cannot be falsified is a temperament rather than an analysis.

  • Central bank demand would have to fall away, not for a quarter but for several years, and the survey evidence would have to reverse. A sustained drop below 200 tonnes a quarter across multiple reporting institutions would begin to test the thesis; a revision of one quarter does not.
  • Mine supply would have to surprise upward in a way that current project pipelines do not anticipate. This is possible but would require a wave of permitting reform across several jurisdictions, which is a political question rather than a geological one and is therefore slower and less predictable than the geology.
  • Industrial substitution would have to accelerate sharply in the applications where it is currently difficult. There is real work underway on reducing silver loading in photovoltaics and on copper-silver hybrids in some connectors, and it deserves more attention than it gets. If a genuinely cheap substitute emerged for high-voltage contacts, a meaningful part of the structural demand case would weaken.
  • The fiscal arithmetic would have to improve in the major economies, which would reduce the case for holding an asset with no counterparty. On current projections this requires either sustained growth above trend or a political willingness to raise taxes and cut spending simultaneously, and neither is presently visible.

The argument, honestly stated, rests on three legs - sovereign accumulation, physical deficit, and fiscal deterioration - and it would take the failure of at least two to make it wrong. A single leg giving way would be survivable. All three failing within the same decade would be close to a refutation, and anyone who insists that cannot happen is overstating the case in the opposite direction.

title: Why Have Saudi Air Defenses Failed To Intercept Houthi Missiles?
desc:
Why Have Saudi Air Defenses Failed To Intercept Houthi Missiles?

Via Middle East Eye

For years, Yemen's Houthis have demonstrated their ability to strike some of Saudi Arabia's most strategically important targets, from oil infrastructure to the kingdom's capital. But repeated missile and drone strikes on Riyadh's main international airport have raised fresh questions about the limits of the kingdom's sophisticated air defenses.

Since October 6, the strikes have killed at least 20 people and injured almost 400. The deadliest attack so far happened on 10 October when 12 people were killed and more than 300 wounded.

On Monday, the kingdom vowed a "serious" response to the attacks and less than 24 hours later, Saudi strikes targeted energy facilities in Sanaa - causing massive fires and explosions that rocked the Yemeni capital.

So why have the latest Houthi attacks repeatedly penetrated Saudi defenses, and what do they reveal about the kingdom's ability to protect its most valuable assets?

Riyadh has spent billions of dollars on some of the world's most advanced air-defense systems, assembling an arsenal designed to counter precisely these threats. Its equipment includes the American-made MIM-104 Patriot, including the advanced PAC-3 variant with hit-to-kill technology, and the even more sophisticated Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system.

Both can intercept ballistic missiles and have demonstrated their capabilities in combat. Saudi Arabia also has a well-equipped air force, including advanced F-15s and Eurofighter Typhoons, capable of engaging drones and cruise missiles.

Yet Houthi missiles and drones have repeatedly evaded or penetrated the kingdom's defenses, exposing the difficulty of protecting a vast territory and its high-value targets from sustained attacks.

Nicholas Heras, interim executive director at the Middle East Policy Council and senior director at the New Lines Institute, said Saudi Arabia's vast territory leaves it "unusually exposed" to Houthi attacks launched from northern Yemen.

"Much of Saudi territory is desert, which makes it challenging to fully defend because of the distances that must be accounted for - and it costs more to have personnel maintain early warning systems in that terrain," Heras told Middle East Eye.

"The Houthis have a target-rich environment in Saudi Arabia that includes some of the most important oil infrastructure in the world that are more immediately exposed to the drone and missile attack capabilities that the Houthis possess."

Heras said the attacks on Riyadh were intended to send a message to Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.

"The Houthis perceived a gap in Saudi capability and attention span and struck Riyadh to send a signal to Saudi Arabia that if Sanaa is hit, Riyadh will be hit," he said.

'Deliberate escalation'

Federico Borsari, a defense expert at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (Cepa), believes the strikes represent an escalation in the Yemeni group’ willingness to attack the kingdom rather than necessarily demonstrating a fundamentally new capability.

The group has possessed long-range strike capabilities for almost a decade and previously targeted Riyadh in 2017. "Since then, their arsenal has further expanded to include increasingly sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles built with Iranian help," Borsari told MEE. "But without evidence it is hard to tell whether some new capabilities were used."

For Borsari, the more concerning development "is the Houthis' ability to conduct repeated, coordinated strikes against heavily defended targets." He added that the timing appears consistent with "deliberate escalation intended to impose economic and political costs" on Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.

Freddy Khoueiry, lead Middle East and North Africa and defense analyst at risk intelligence company RANE, said it remained unclear whether the attacks reflected new Houthi capabilities.

"Based on publicly available information, it is still difficult to determine whether the Riyadh attacks represent a specific new technological upgrade or simply a decision to employ existing capabilities more aggressively against civilian aviation infrastructure," he told MEE. "In either case, the escalation is significant because the Houthis are demonstrating both the capability and willingness to impose direct costs on the Saudi capital," he said.

Mohammed al-Basha of the Virginia-based Basha Report risk advisory said the Houthis had spent years refining their long-range strike capabilities. "For years, the Houthis have used their attacks on Israel to refine their long-range strike capabilities," he told MEE. "What appeared to be failed attacks were also opportunities to learn and adapt."

The group may have applied lessons from its regional attacks, as well as from Iran’s confrontations with the US and Israel, to improve its ability to challenge sophisticated air-defence networks. "Saudi Arabia has invested heavily in Patriot, Thaad, and other systems, but its vast territory makes comprehensive protection difficult," al-Basha said.

"The Houthis do not need to overwhelm the entire network. One successful strike can cause significant damage and disruption."

Newly released footage shows blasts near airport seating at Abha, damage to the ceiling at Jazan and debris falling inside Najran International Airport. Saudi officials blame Houthi attacks for the destruction, reporting three people killed and 28 wounded in strikes on Abha airport alone. The attacks are part of a broader campaign targeting Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities.

— Fox News (@FoxNews) October 16, 2026

The repeated strikes also raise questions about whether Saudi Arabia has enough interceptors to sustain its defences during a prolonged campaign.

The interceptor problem

Saudi Arabia's interceptor stockpiles may have been depleted following sustained use during the wider regional conflict with Iran. Repeated missile and drone attacks can rapidly consume the expensive interceptors needed to stop incoming threats.

The United States has also expended significant quantities of Patriot and Thaad interceptors during the conflict, putting pressure on supplies that could take years to replenish.

Borsari described interceptor depletion as a "credible explanation" for the breaches, although he cautioned against treating it as the only possible cause. He pointed to media reports from last month suggesting that Riyadh was running low on ballistic missile interceptors.

"If true, this would create difficult operational trade-offs for air-defense commanders when deciding which threats to engage, how many interceptors to allocate, etc," he said. "These decisions become even more problematic during mass salvos."

The Houthis could also be attempting to saturate Saudi defenses by launching different types of weapons simultaneously, including one-way attack drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles. Even sophisticated, multilayered air-defense systems cannot guarantee that every incoming projectile will be intercepted during a sustained bombardment.

Borsari said it would be "naive to deny" that the Riyadh strikes raise "serious questions" about the effectiveness of Saudi Arabia’s ballistic missile defences, particularly their ability to protect fixed, high-value targets under repeated attack.

Khoueiry similarly argued that the strikes were less evidence of "a fundamental deficiency" in Saudi air defences than a reminder of the limitations facing even advanced systems. "Saudi Arabia has to defend a very large territory and prioritize coverage around major cities, military sites and critical infrastructure, while interceptor availability is also under pressure," he said. "Direct ballistic-missile impacts could reflect those constraints, but on their own they do not prove a severe interceptor shortage."

A costly game of adaptation

"We don't know what the specific cause of this failure is," Borsari said of the attacks. He noted that an air defense network's effectiveness depends on several components. "The effectiveness of a defensive network depends not simply on the sophistication of its interceptors but also on sensor coverage and integration, proficient C2 (command and control), ammunition availability, etc. So it could be any of these, or - most likely - a combination thereof."

Saudi Arabia's geography compounds those challenges. Its airports, oil facilities, ports and military installations are spread across a vast area, making continuous protection expensive and difficult to sustain.

"The main challenge is detection, and for that you need to rely on various assets, including aircraft, to ensure proper early warning," Borsari said. "But maintaining such a detection regime over time is very costly and a sustainment burden on both the equipment and personnel."

There are cheaper options for countering drones in particular, including automated anti-drone turrets equipped with heavy machine guns and low-cost short-range interceptors. But these require supporting infrastructure and careful integration with existing systems.

"So I'm afraid we will continue to see drones penetrating Saudi territory for the foreseeable future," Borsari said.

Khoueiry sees the latest Houthi strikes, alongside recent Iranian attacks on American and regional targets, as evidence of a wider effort to adapt to sophisticated air-defense systems rather than simply a matter of luck. "Iran and its partners appear to be learning how to operate against layered air defense networks, adapting flight routes and tactics to improve penetration and impose higher interception and economic costs," he said.

"The lesson for Saudi Arabia and the wider region is that increasingly sophisticated air defenses still need dense surveillance, sufficient interceptor stocks and constant adaptation to keep pace with evolving missile and drone threats."

title: A Horror Movie List To Get You In The Mood For Spooky Season
desc:
A Horror Movie List To Get You In The Mood For Spooky Season

The horror entertainment genre is a lot like comedy - Both require deep immersion and instinctive reactions. Being browbeaten with overt political messaging in the middle of such films ruins them completely. Nobody wants to hear a feminist sermon in the middle of Texas Chainsaw Massacre, they just want to watch that messed up dinner table scene.

Parable and subtle messaging is fine, but propaganda is not.

With Hollywood slowly but surely sinking into a shallow grave with little hope of escape, the industry has desperately turned to the old mainstay of horror to save the box office. Why? Because it's cheap, fast and thrives on the imagination of indie auteurs willing to engage in risky storytelling. In a world of endless remakes, reboots and "re-imaginings", audiences are desperate for something original.

And, as long as that original film isn't disgustingly ripe with leftist propaganda, everyone is generally happy.

There's not enough new and good horror productions to fill out this list of spooky season primers, but there's a few, along with some lesser known classics to get in the mood for Halloween. Let's start with the best new horror media...

Obsession

One of the biggest surprise hits of the year, Obsession follows the ill fated efforts of Baron Baily to gain the attention of his attractive co-worker Nikki Freeman. His inability to escape the "friend zone" leads him to a cursed novelty item called the "One Wish Willow". His innocent wish for Nikki to fall in love with him results in her darkly hilarious (but ultimately grotesque and disturbing) obsession with him.

The film has the obvious "careful what you wish for" horror narrative, but it gets a lot more complicated. The story stands as a perfect allegory for Gen Z men's fears over "MeToo" and the feminist culture of accusation, without ever mentioning the issue or the politics. It explores the idea of romance vs infatuation and control.

Finally, it depicts a subject matter which is rarely ever portrayed on film anymore; the weakness of beta men and their refusal to break with toxic women because they are terrified over the stigma of being alone more than the ticking time bomb that is their relationship. Like many of the films on this list, there's a element of tragic humor to this movie that sets it apart from the more lazy nihilist stories that have flooded the horror genre lately.

Widow's Bay

It's a streaming series and not a movie, but a perfect watch for the month of October. Widow's Bay is one of the few Apple TV productions actually worth a damn and one can only hope that it gets a second season despite being buried on that lifeless platform.

The series focuses on Mayor Tom Loftis, a struggling middle-aged widower trying to take care of his petulant and sometimes sociopathic teenage son in an island community oppressed by superstitious fears. It is said that anyone born on the island will die if they try to leave. The island will not let them escape.

Tom was not born on the island and doesn't believe that the place is cursed, so he attempts to rebrand Widow's Bay as a tourist destination similar to Martha's Vineyard. Hilarity and horror ensues.

The show is a mix between Parks And Recreation and The X Files with various homages to the classic horror movies of the 1980s and 1990s. It is also one of the funniest series produced in a long time, while still being extremely effective at building up supernatural dread. Each episode acts as a self contained horror tale, but the through-line plot holds together perfectly. All the characters on the island are fantastically written and fantastically weird, and the series climax is a compelling cliffhanger.

Buddy

It's strange to admit it, but this low budget parody of the 1990s "Barney" kids show might just be one of the best and most disturbing horror movies of the past decade.

Buddy is another film that is simultaneously funny and uncomfortable, you're not sure whether you're supposed to laugh or pull back in revulsion as the classic kids show filled with puppets, dancing and singing descends into a nightmare world where the children are in danger of being murdered by a rampaging homicidal supernatural unicorn.

This one is for horror fans who love to step outside of their comfort zone and it's definitely not a family film. The story plays with idea of the thin veil of reality far more effectively than the "Backrooms" flick, and gets so weird you have to admire the level of imagination it took to devise the blood curdling events that unfold.

One is immediately reminded of Peter Jackson (director of Lord Of The Rings) and his early films like "Dead Alive" and "Bad Taste". But most of all, Buddy seems to take a lot from Jackson's film "Meet The Feebles", a disturbing satire of Sesame Street and the Muppet Show in which a bunch of innocent show tunes puppets engage in increasingly depraved situations. There is also an element of the YouTube series "Don't Hug Me I'm Scared" - If you know, you know.

Oddity

Not exactly a brand new film (produced in 2024), but this movie fell by the wayside in the midst of a politically contentious year when it should have gotten more attention. This Irish horror flick is absolutely chilling, combining a murder mystery with a ghost story.

A well-to-do woman is brutally murdered while refurbishing an old estate in the Irish countryside. Her twin sister who has clairvoyant abilities, Darcy Odello, travels to the property to uncover the facts behind the case. She also carries with her a creepy wooden mannequin.

The build-up in this movie is expertly crafted and every element of it screams Halloween.

Older And Lesser Known Classics

If you're tired of watching the same standard Halloween movies every year, here are some ideas to spice up your spooky season watch list...

The Innocents

A more obscure but well loved cult classic; The Innocents is a beautifully filmed black-and-white gothic ghost tale produced in 1961 about a Governess (Miss Giddens) hired by a wealthy patron to watch over two orphaned children who seem normal at first, but start to act very strangely.

Like most supernatural movies of this time period, the story is a slow burn with creepy atmosphere. The horror comes from the ambiguity and the audience not knowing if what the main character is experiencing is real. Is Miss Giddens seeing ghosts? Are the children possessed? Or, is she losing her sanity?

In The Mouth Of Madness

A cult classic that is getting a lot more attention in recent years, John Carpenter's "In The Mouth Of Madness" is a lot like his film "The Thing". Audiences just didn't understand the genius of it at the time. It took a few decades before people were finally ready.

The movie is an homage to the interdimensional horror of H.P. Lovecraft which asks: What if our world was nothing more than a thin barrier between humanity and a dark realm where creatures older than time reside, waiting to break through and devour everything? What if, through our own bungling, we ended up tearing a hole into that terrible place?

In The Mouth If Madness has all the dark humor Carpenter is known for along with a more unfamiliar foray into cosmic horror.

Dead Alive (a.k.a Braindead)

Before Peter Jackson went down in film history for his beloved Lord Of The Rings trilogy, he was better known for making some of the weirdest and most disgusting low budget horror films of all time. The pinnacle of these films has to be "Dead Alive", also known as "Braindead".

An overzealous zoo keeper hijacks a cursed "Sumatran Rat Monkey" from forbidden tribal grounds and sends it to New Zealand, where it ends up biting the psychopathic mother of Lionel Cosgrove. The poor guy is already held hostage by the overbearing old woman and she sabotages him every time he meets a nice girl. But now, she's turning into some kind of undead creature, and the rest of the town will follow if he doesn't man up and fight back.

Will his newfound love for local grocery girl Paquita Sanchez help him to defeat an invasion from hell?

This movie is an unbelievable gore fest and for strong stomachs only. Also famous for the line: "I kick ass for the Lord!"

The Blob (1988 Remake)

Another gore fest, but with more traditional storytelling, is a remake of the 1958 classic starring Steve McQueen. This version is far more frightening and the incredible practical effects make you long for the days before everything was lazy and CG.

A rebellious small town teen (Brian Flagg) must use his cunning to stop the invasion of a formless gooey invader that uses acid to envelop and digest every living thing it touches. He also has to contend with a government agency that might not have the best interests of the town in mind.

The Witches

Based on Roald Dahl's dark fantasy novel, "The Witches" (1990 version) follows Luke, a young boy who lost his parents in a terrible accident. Luke goes to live with his eccentric but loving grandmother (Helga) who tells him scary stories about the hidden world of witches. Unlike the more innocuous and cartoonish characters of popular fiction, Helga warns Luke that witches are, in fact, real, and they are murderous monsters who prey on children.

When Luke and his Grandmother travel to a seaside hotel, Luke realizes that his grandmother was right - The resort is infested with hideous witches disguised as normal women, and they're hatching an evil plot to kill thousands of innocent kids. Unfortunately, they turn him into a mouse before he can warn anyone.

Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and early 1990s probably remembers this film, but it has faded as a Halloween classic in recent years. Perhaps because it is a family film, but like many kids movies of the era, it doesn't pull any punches with the scares. The concept of a boy and his grandmother hunting down evil witches is by itself worth a watch.

title: The Future Of American Drone Warfare
desc:
The Future Of American Drone Warfare

Authored by Adam Sharp via The Daily Reckoning,

While the war with Iran might be nearing a resolution, the war in Ukraine is heating up.

Whether this is the next stage in escalation, or the grand finale remains unclear. But lessons continue to emerge from this conflict, and world powers are beginning to act on them at scale.

Ukrainian long-range drones continue to hammer Russian energy and military sites. Targets up to 1,700 kilometers inside Russia are being hit.

A Ukrainian long-range drone. Source: AP

These strikes are causing serious economic damage to Russia, not to mention the environmental harm. Here's a screenshot of recent fires at Russia's Rosneft facility on the Black Sea after Ukrainian drone attacks.

Source: X

Earlier this week, President Trump expressed his anger at Ukrainian President Zelensky, "It's time for Ukraine to get a NEW PRESIDENT!"

Ukraine's strikes are hammering Russia's fuel production, and causing shortages worldwide.

On the front lines, short-range drones are now Ukraine's primary weapon holding back Russian advances. Most of these are small drones with anti-tank RPG warheads attached.

Crude, but highly effective. There are also bomber drones which drop grenades, mortars, and improvised munitions. Interceptor drones roam the skies, looking to foil enemy attacks.

Both sides are using flamethrower drones, which drip molten thermite to melt anti-drone netting and ignite enemy structures.

Meanwhile Russian long-range drones and missiles are increasingly hitting military sites in the capital, Kiev (Kyiv). And across the rest of the country. Glide bombs are devastating the front lines. And Russia is using at least as many short-range drones as Ukraine is.

It is estimated that up to 15,000 drones are being used in Ukraine per day. And that up to 90% of casualties are caused by these terrible little machines.

Traditional maneuver warfare is extremely difficult in these conditions. Advances crawl forward at a snail's pace.

Tanks and IFVs are increasingly irrelevant on the battlefield. Even artillery, the "God of War", has become an afterthought.

In just a few short years, this new class of drones have changed warfare forever. The question is: are American defense contractors ready for this new world?

Petraeus' Warning

Former Army General and CIA Director David Petraeus is out with a new warning about drone warfare. I'm not a fan of the man, but what he says here is true.

"We have not remotely learned all the lessons we should have from the war in Ukraine.

That is the future of war right now. Ukraine is using 10,000 drones a day.

Ninety percent of the casualties on the Russian side are caused by drones. Tanks can't manoeuvre anymore. They can't survive. Armored vehicles can't survive.

And by the way, there's more coming. Within a year or two, we're going to see unmanned systems that are not remotely piloted.

In the future, we're going to see autonomous systems - truly autonomous - that do not require a pilot to remotely operate them.

Then you face drone swarms. And that is something for which we really don't have a solution."

Weapons Giants Fall Behind

America's largest defense contractors, Lockheed Martin (LMT) and Northrop Grumman (NOC), have traditionally focused on gigantic programs. The F-35, naval ships, helicopters, cruise missiles, and big drones costing $30-90 million a piece.

These contractors have been forced to build their supply chains and manufacturing around getting support from specific political districts.

Elon Musk has been especially critical of U.S. defense firms, singling out manned fighter jets like the F-35 as "obsolete in the age of drones."

Source: X

I'm not sure fighter jets are obsolete just yet. But tanks and other traditional weapons systems do seem to be moving in that direction.

The point is that making cheap disposable "kamikaze" drones at scale is outside the wheelhouse of big defense firms.

Now that the U.S. military wants low-cost attack drones, they are doing something unusual: going to smaller firms in search of innovation.

New Drone Depots

The U.S. military is converting 6 Army depots into drone production facilities across the country. Defense Post:

The McAlester Army Ammunition Plant (MCAAP) in Oklahoma is adapting its munitions production to support modern drone warfare through a new partnership with Perennial Autonomy.

They're partnering with various private companies to build drone manufacturing capabilities domestically. Beefing up our drone production base is key to modernizing the military.

Especially because the government's requirements call for doing it without any Chinese parts.

That in itself is a huge challenge, because today China makes about 85% of the world's commercial and personal drones. China's supply chains are already incredibly developed, and it will take time to build out our own. The vast majority of Ukrainian and Russian drones used are either Chinese, or built with Chinese motors, batteries, servos, and other parts.

The Drone Dominance Program

It's been nearly 5 years since the war in Ukraine began, and the disruptive potential of drone warfare became clear.

The U.S. Department of War is now beginning to ramp up drone programs. In Iran we saw the debut of the LUCAS attack drone, based on Iran's Shahed-136.

Now the American military is looking to build 300,000 attack drones by 2028. That may sound like a lot, but it's 15 days of supply for Russia and Ukraine.

The Drone Dominance Program (DDP) is a fascinating development. The Department of War is tearing up the old playbook of 10-30 year development cycles and trying something fresh.

Dozens of companies were invited to participate in a series of trials. Various drones are tested for accuracy, speed, resistance to electronic warfare, and other objectives.

And the Department of War has an online leaderboard showing the top performers:

Source: Drone Dominance official site

Note the complete absence of any big defense contractors. The leading performer, Skycutter, is a small private U.K. company with plenty of frontline experience in Ukraine.

We are early in this new age of drone warfare. But it is set to shake up America's stale defense contracting business. New players are emerging.

The legacy defense giants have been slow to adapt to this reality. They remain focused on cash cow programs.

And for a while, that playbook will work. But the future of warfare looks like it will be dominated by unmanned systems. And the big, slow, expensive drones they make today are clearly not cut out for this new world.

American defense giants have coasted for decades on gold-plated billion-dollar contracts. They have failed to produce effective hypersonic missiles and affordable attack drones. Their reign won't last forever.

I'll be watching to see which companies emerge as leaders in this new tech. Many of them are private startups at this point, so aren't investable (yet).

But disruption is finally coming to the defense industry. It's about time.

title: "We have A Zero-Tolerance Policy": High School Student "Punished" For Expressing Support For The 'Cornell 7'
desc:
"We have A Zero-Tolerance Policy": High School Student "Punished" For Expressing Support For The 'Cornell 7'

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

We have previously discussed high school administrators and teachers who engage in censorship and speech regulation, often targeting religious and conservative students. These cases cost school districts millions in court costs, but the school officials never seem to face any consequences. In California, Piner High School has joined this ignoble effort, punishing the high school football captain for expressing support for the "Cornell 7" on his own Instagram page. Other students then protested not to support free speech but to demand further punishment for the student. I wonder where they learned that repressive view of free speech?

According to media reports, the unnamed student wrote "Free the Cornell Seven" on his personal Instagram account and the school called him out. As should be obvious to any teacher or administrator, this is entirely protected speech under the First Amendment. The student was not discussing the school, calling for some school disruption or destruction of property, or encouraging violence. He was stating his view that defendants who have not been tried, let alone convicted, are innocent.

This case has divided the country with many politicians and pundits declaring the guilt of these students before any charges are actually filed against them. A prosecutor previously declined to take the case to a grand jury due to conflict statements from the alleged victim.

Rather than acknowledge the serious free speech concerns raised by the school's reported actions, Santa Rosa City school's public information officer, Patrick Gannon, issued a virtue-signaling statement on how it will not tolerate students expressing such thoughts on their personal social media accounts, or presumably publicly in their private time:

"Action was taken by the school and the district, and we're continuing to have conversations. We don't tolerate making light of sexual assault. That's why we have a zero-tolerance policy."

Whatever success the school has had on basic subjects like English and Math, it has clearly taught the student body to disregard the free speech of others. The football team reportedly forfeited a game after 200 students walked out to the "Santa Rosa City Schools district offices to demand accountability and greater support for students speaking out against sexual violence."

There was no statement from Principal Andrea Correia or the school denying the reported punishment. Instead, Gannon met with the 200 students and, instead of discussing the importance of free speech and due process, said the school "wants them to know that accountability and safety are top priorities."

Students are demanding further punishment of the student for expressing his views on the case. Obviously, if the same students had posted "Justice for Jane Doe at Cornell" he would have been celebrated rather than punished.

In 1969, the Supreme Court famously declared that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." However, since that iconic case, federal courts have often given short shrift to the free speech rights of students.

As we have previously discussed, teachers around the country have become notorious as speech commissars who bar expressions deemed divisive or intolerant. That often includes any conservative or religious speech.

An elementary school in Kansas came under fire after Arbor Creek Elementary Principal Melissa Snell stopped the wearing of shirts reading "Freedom," which became popular after the assassination of Charlie Kirk.

In another case, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Boyko ruled in Ohio that students could be barred from wearing "Let's Go Brandon" shirts - a coded political expression criticizing the media and former President Joe Biden. Other courts have also upheld such censorship by teachers, who claim that the expression is a substitute for a vulgar expression chanted by crowds ("F- Joe Biden"). But these shirts do not contain vulgarity. Rather, the expression is used as a defiant reference to the media bias that led to the original substitution of the words, allegedly to protect Biden - it is a "Yankee Doodling" of the political and media establishment.

Judge Karen Nelson Moore joined Sixth Circuit Judge John Nalbandian in a deeply flawed holding that, under the "vulgarity exception," the action was constitutional. The Supreme Court was asked to hear the "Let's Go Brandon" case, but recently declined to hear the case. It was a very disappointing denial from the Court for many of us in the free speech community.

In the California case, the underlying law is clear. Any punishment of this student would be a glaring violation of the First Amendment. The student can go to court to have any such actions set aside. However, it is equally clear that the administrators and teachers responsible for such actions will face no accountability.

The "zero tolerance policy" at Piner High School appears to refer to the exercise of free speech by those with unpopular or minority viewpoints. It is certainly a preview of higher education, where viewpoint intolerance and ideological orthodoxy are the norm. This chilling lesson has clearly taken hold at Piner High School.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution."
